No hygiene, no sexual health, and frighteningly, no choice as to when to have a child - in breach of the Genocide Convention. ]]> Despite a heinous campaign displacing over 90 percent of the strip’s population, there are some members of Gaza society that have been bearing the brunt of the deterioration more than others. 

Anyone needing to use a toilet in the demolished Palestinian territory must usually sit through long queues near a displacement encampment, where the debris of a former school may eventually play host to their needs. Often, however, the squatted toilet is no more than just a hole in the ground. 

That has presented profound difficulty for menstruating or pregnant women. 

Some women’s groups have attempted to cover the massive chasm left behind by three years of continued Israeli bombardment of any health structure, while emergency aid remains blockaded outside of Gaza.

Read more

Lead trade MEP Bernd Lange slams EU Commission for ‘hiding’ behind voting rules on banning Israeli settlement imports

A new report by Amnesty International to be published on Wednesday (25 November) found the gendered impact of Israel’s ongoing violence in Gaza on women and girls to including the virtual absence of hygiene products and essential healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health.

And in a climate of constant aggression, women are bearing the brunt of an increased risk of gender-based violence. 

While forced to grieve and face the impossible challenge of sourcing food for their families every day, Gaza’s women are facing the toll of increased sexual and occupation-sourced violence, fuelled by the complete collapse of institutional justice systems, and the erosion of community and family protection.

]]> ‘Null and void’: EU rejects Libya-Turkey pact that could allow oil drilling in Greek waters https://euobserver.com/251216/null-and-void-eu-rejects-libya-turkey-pact-that-could-allow-oil-drilling-in-greek-waters/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:22:17 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251216 The EU has flatly rejected a maritime deal between Turkey and Libya - but it poses a major headache for its relations with both countries.]]> The EU has rejected as “null and void” a controversial maritime pact between Turkey and Libya that is bitterly opposed by Greece and could pave the way for Turkish oil and gas exploration close to Crete. 

The memorandum proposes a maritime corridor across the eastern Mediterranean from north-east Libya to south-west Turkey, and would create an avenue for Turkey and Libya to conduct potentially lucrative joint gas exploration and drilling operations. 

Greece argues, with the support of both the EU and United Nations, that the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) breaches Greek sovereignty over waters surrounding the island of Crete and its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). 

The EU’s Mediterranean commissioner Dubravka Šuica told MEPs in Strasbourg on Tuesday (24 November) that the memorandum “does not comply with the law of the society…it is null and void”, adding that the EU Commission “reiterates full solidarity with Greece and Cyprus.” 

The commission had “consistently reflected these concerns to Turkey”, she said. 

The maritime deal was originally agreed between Turkey and the Tripoli based Government of National Accord, which has been recognised as Libya’s government by the EU and most of the international community.

But it was opposed by general Khalifa Haftar, the leader of the Libyan National Army, which has operated a rival administration in eastern Libya. 

But in October, the Tobruk-based House of Representatives, backed in Haftar, approved the memorandum, paving the way for Turkish firms to start oil and gas exploration.

]]> MEPs still split over ending Hungary’s Article 7 sanctions procedure, but Magyar’s reforms win praise https://euobserver.com/251017/meps-still-split-over-ending-hungarys-article-7-sanctions-procedure-as-magyars-reforms-win-praise/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:13:10 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251017 Unfreezing EU funds to encourage progress on the democratic reforms of the new Hungarian government were a good step, most MEPs said in a plenary debate, despite cries of ‘double standards’ from the right.]]> The centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), the European Parliament’s largest group, says Hungary is no longer breaching EU core values and is pushing to end the ‘Article 7’ sanctions proceedings – but other groups warn the job isn’t finished, setting up a tight December vote to close the file. 

Acknowledging that “years of damage cannot be undone in just six months,” centre-right Swedish MEP Tomas Tobé (EPP) welcomed the progress since Péter Magyar’s centre-right government won the parliamentary elections in April, ending 16 years of Viktor Orbán’s illiberal rule. 

“Progress must be recognised,” he said.

So did the commission earlier this year, when billions of euros in frozen EU cohesion and recovery funds for Hungary were partially unblocked following rule-of-law and anti-corruption reforms. 

“Is everything perfect? Of course not, but the political will is there,” also said Belgian liberal MEP and former prime minister Sophie Wilmès during the debate.

Read more

EU Commission ‘confident’ that Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia will join new €45bn Ukraine loan

“We kept banging against the same wall: Viktor Orbán. In April, Hungarians themselves broke down this wall,” she said, adding that, in response, the EU Parliament should send Hungarians a “positive signal of encouragement.”

But a Polish centre-left MEP, Krzysztof Śmiszek, said that while the current reforms were “important,” they were not enough to say there was no “threat to rule of law.”

German Green MEP Daniel Freund has also warned against closing the EU’s rule-of-law procedure just yet, warning that Hungary still fails to comply with an EU asylum ruling.

Magyar’s new government has already made “extraordinary progress “, but “many tasks still lie ahead [to uphold EU values],” also said Tineke Strik, a Green MEP leading the parliament’s work on Hungary rule of law.

“We owe it to Hungarian people to be diligent in our assessment”, she added.

In 2018, the European Parliament triggered the EU treaty’s Article 7 procedure against Hungary over serious rule of law breaches, which could have ultimately resulted in sanctions such as suspending Hungary’s voting rights in the Council.

But this never happened – neither to Hungary nor to Poland, the only two countries which have ever been under the Article 7 procedure, given the need for unanimous support and amid fears of retaliation by other rightwing governments. 

To formally end the Article 7 procedure, MEPs must vote to withdraw it, and that decision requires a two-thirds majority, meaning at least 480 of the parliament’s 719 lawmakers, before the council, representing member states, can close the file.

Read more

Hungary digs up €17m in buried cash during probe into Orbán-era minister Seszták

Meanwhile, despite rule-of-law breaches and the dismantling of democratic institutions in Hungary, Orbán’s Fidesz party was a member of the EPP group until 2021, which triggered criticism from left-wing MEPs during Tuesday’s debate in Strasbourg.

]]> Nathan Cofnas is just the latest far-right ‘snowflake’ to pretend he’s being martyred in Europe https://euobserver.com/251088/nathan-cofnas-is-just-the-latest-far-right-snowflake-to-pretend-hes-being-martyred-in-europe/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:53:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251088 Pro-Russian and far-right snowflakes are crying about being cancelled in the EU, but their shtick is getting old and boring, just like the manosphere and anti-vaxers who first wrote the script.]]> Pro-Russian and far-right snowflakes are crying about being cancelled in the EU, but their shtick is getting old and boring, just like the manosphere and anti-vaxers who first wrote the script.

One of them, Irishman Chay Bowes, has been all over my X-feed since 16 November, when the EU blacklisted him for doing Russian propaganda.

Another one, EU-listed Russian propagandist and Belgian resident Thomas Baud, had his Austrian lawyers set up an interview with me in March.

Yet another one, racist US academic Nathan Cofnas, was briefing press in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday (24 November) on how he was “cancelled at university [in the Netherlands] for telling the truth”, by which he meant his view that black people are stupider than white people, and claiming that an Arab MEP tried to stop his press stunt because he is “Zionist”.

For their part, Bowes and Baud cannot travel to or through EU states outside Ireland or Belgium, respectively, access their bank accounts, or make electronic payments, as they are under EU visa-bans and asset-freezes.

The same EU sanctions apply to French media figures Adrien Bocquet and Xavier Moraeu, and German ones Hüseyin Dogru, Alina Lipp, and Thomas Röper.

Bowes is crying that this is an “Orwellian” EU assault on his free speech and that some overcautious firms had declined his relatives’ payments too.

Baud and his lawyers went on and on in the same vein for over two hours in Zoom and WhatsApp calls, while he also tried to use EUobserver to plug his books and YouTube channel.

Cofnas merely lost his job, but is now auditioning to be a far-right pin-up, as you can tell from the AI-sculpted jawline on his cherubic face in his EU Parliament press release.

All the self-declared martyrs have a supporting chorus of pro-Russian and far-right MEPs in Brussels and MPs in EU capitals.

All of them are being megaphoned by US tech billionaires, who are aligned with the pro-Russian and far-right US president, and by Russian troll and bot farms.

And their myths are helped to go viral by far-right influencers, by the stars of the online manosphere, and also by far-left conspiracy theorists (of the kind who said Covid was a totalitarian hoax), as well as the broader spectrum of climate-change deniers and flat-earthers to which all this slop belongs.

British influencer, accused rapist, and pro-Kremlin propagandist Andrew Tate was an archetypal martyr of the kind, who blamed the deep state for booting him off the internet.

And British convicted rapist, Russophile, and anti-vaxer Russell Brand was another fellow traveller, who is now being painted as a crucified messiah by his fans.

]]> Some 720,000 Russian soldiers killed in the war, in leaked data deemed authentic by the independent Mediazona news website (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,734) https://euobserver.com/251050/some-720000-russian-soldiers-killed-in-the-war-in-leaked-data-deemed-authentic-by-the-independent-mediazona-news-website-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1734/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:46:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251050 The newly authenticated death rolls show a war hollowing out Russia’s working-age male population, stripping poor regions of fathers and breadwinners at a pace that already eclipses all Soviet conflicts since 1945. ]]>
  • Mediazona has verified data from a leak from Russia’s statistical agency — it is authentic.
  • It is certain that at least 490,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war. The actual figure, however, is estimated at 720,000 dead.
  • The data confirm that the age of soldiers killed is increasing, as is the fact that they come from poor regions. The highest number died near Bakhmut and Pokrovsk.
  • Recruitment apparently cannot keep pace with current losses: this year, Russia signed up 10 percent fewer men than last year.
  • Map of the day: Dobropillia.
  • Videos of the day: an Abrams tank adapted for modern warfare; a strike on central Zaporizhzhia; Russians built scaffolding around facilities at a refinery in Perm; it apparently did not help.

    • Two weeks ago, we wrote about data that Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers had stolen from Russia’s statistical agency, Rosstat. The data concerned deceased Russian citizens from 2021 to the end of August 2026.

    From these data, both groups concluded that between 400,000 and 450,000 Russians had been killed in the war. It was still not clear, however, whether the data were authentic — Russian sources had previously also published similar leaks claiming enormous, and therefore implausible, Ukrainian losses.

    However, the hacker groups Cyber Partisan and Silent Crow provided the data to various media outlets. They are now freely accessible to the public (the files total 365 gigabytes).

    It was awaited what the Russian independent website Mediazona, which has long searched for and catalogued the deaths of Russian soldiers through obituaries, official documents and other sources, would say about the data.

    On Monday evening, the Russian website published its analysis of the data.

    Mediazona’s journalists have no doubt that the Rosstat leak contains authentic data on real people who died in the war. They compared it with their own data. They found 95 percent of “their” soldiers in Rosstat’s records.

    “We are convinced that these data are authentic: they were verified using a list of the names of the deceased, including records not previously published, the register of inheritance proceedings, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court rulings from publicly available sources, and data previously published by Rosstat itself,” Mediazona wrote.

    The analysis of these data suggests that the total number of Russian soldiers killed is even higher than previously estimated.

Its findings also show that some doctors upload sensitive patient data to commercial AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini without approval, and that hospitals struggle to comply with overlapping EU rules on privacy and AI.]]> Hospitals depend on AI they do not control, while EU-funded health startups rarely reach public hospitals in Europe, a report published on Tuesday (24 November) reveals.

    Its findings also show that doctors facing burnout often upload sensitive patient data to commercial AI chatbots without approval, and that hospitals struggle to comply with overlapping EU rules on privacy and AI.

    The EU previously identified healthcare as one of 10 strategic sectors to boost European competitiveness. “I wanted to find out if the EU’s ambitions around scaling health AI and developing truly sovereign European health AI tools really hold up in practice,” lead researcher Júlia Keserű told EUobserver in an interview. 

    Her analysis was run in partnership with Liberties, a human rights watchdog, and was supported by The Collaborative for AI in the Public Interest, a philanthropic project by eBay’s founder.

    The research included interviews with more than 50 hospital workers, scholars and patient advocates, whose insights exposed the struggle of the health sector to comply with EU rules on data privacy and artificial intelligence.

    “There are too many rules and they are too complicated,” Keserű said, explaining that hospitals struggle to comply with rules that are often overlapping and contradictory.

    And while the privacy rights researcher calls for “harmonisation” of rules, she warned that “if simplification means cutting baseline protections for patients, it creates new risks.”

    ‘Careless’ use of AI by stressed doctors

    Among the concerns raised by Keserű’s interviewees, the most prominent was the use of ‘shadow AI’, where clinicians paste potentially sensitive patient data into commercial generative AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini without approval from their employers.

Opposition leaders accuse them of brazenly rewriting the rules to shut out hostile voters before the next election. ]]> Slovakia’s parliament voted on Tuesday (24 November) on a proposal that would abolish voting by post for its citizens living abroad in parliamentary elections, replacing it with in-person voting at Slovak embassies and consulates.

    In the 2023 elections, almost 59,000 citizens voted by mail, with the current opposition party emerging as the clear winner among them, receiving 62 percent of the votes.

    “Representatives of this coalition had no problem with postal voting for 20 years, until voters made them pay for it in the last election,” Ľudovít Ódor, Slovak MEP for Renew Europe and former prime minister, told EUobserver.

    “Slovaks living abroad are often critical of the current government,” Martin Hojsík, vice-president of the European Parliament and Slovak MEP, told EUobserver. “Which is precisely why this proposal raises serious questions.”

    “It is hard to escape the impression that the governing coalition is not concerned with election security, but rather with who will be allowed to participate in them,” he added.

    The proposal has become controversial not only because of its practical implications for Slovaks living abroad, but also because of the way it has been brought back onto parliament’s agenda – after already failing twice.

    The bill, introduced by prime minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SSD party, had already been removed from the agenda on 16 September and again on 11 November, after neither its sponsors nor the designated rapporteur attended the scheduled debates. Under parliamentary rules, the second failure should have meant that the proposal could not be discussed again for six months.

    “If this amendment is indeed passed, we will take the matter to the Constitutional Court,” Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová, Slovak MEP for Renew Europe, told EUobserver.

    Party-political motives

    As the organisation of elections remains primarily a national competence, EU member states retain discretion over how their citizens exercise their voting rights.

    For Slovak MEPs, it is interesting to see how political parties use these regulations to alter the conditions of political competition and potentially limit the ability of certain groups of citizens to have a say in the direction their country takes.

    “It is clear that this is a politically motivated move,” Miriam Lexmann, a Slovak MEP from the European People’s Party (EPP), told EUobserver.

    Read more

    ‘Manual for autocrats’: how Fico’s rule-of-law breaches put Slovakia in EU sanctions crosshairs

    It is not a new phenomena. For US president Donald Trump, mail-in ballots represent a “massive voter fraud”, he claimed. And Fico’s coalition has also echoed this argument.

    “Trump has claimed that the most recent US elections were manipulated because of postal voting. But there is absolutely no evidence to support these allegations,” Rasťo Kužel executive director at Memo98, international organisation in the field of media and elections, told EUobserver.

    Many other EU democracies such as Germany use postal voting.

    For Kužel, it is a way of dividing the population.

    In this case, “Smer is positioning itself against people who live abroad. This is primarily about further polarising society.”

    The Tuesday (24 November) judgement spanned several separate cases involving Poland, Lithuania and Latvia at a time when Belarus was rounding up people and pushing them across its border, triggering stand-offs with authorities and a tightening of asylum rights.

    While each case had their own individual particularities, ruling in favour of some and against others, the court now allows national authorities to return able-bodied adults to a hostile state if they are unable to prove they face an immediate danger. Small children and the disabled are exempt.

    The distinction is important because it only applies in the context of instrumentalisation, a catch-all phrase used to describe the orchestrated attempts by a government or state to destabilise an EU country.

    Some have accused Morocco of similar tactics, when over 70,000 people suddenly arrived in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July. Turkey has also been similarly accused previously, when thousands arrived in Greece in 2020, laying the framework for a new EU asylum law that is supposed to respond to such scenarios.

    Tuesday’s verdict is likely to complicate the future efforts of those seeking asylum in Europe, as well as weigh in on 30 similar pending cases at the Strasbourg-court.

    It also opens the door for the European Commission to propose new policy later this year to help curb asylum whenever people are being instrumentalised in cases similar to Ceuta.

    Read more

    Poland’s pushback drive and EU asylum ‘emergency’ plan put rights ‘on a cliff edge’, warns Europe’s top rights chief

    Tuesday’s verdict most likely affects young males and other adults.

    French President Emmanuel Macron could revive an idea that has been around for quite some time: introducing a so-called golden rule around public deficit into the French constitution.

    What is it exactly, and how is it different from the EU budgetary rules? The principle of that golden rule would be to require the state to keep its budget more or less balanced. In other words, the government would have to commit to a specific budgetary trajectory, aiming, for instance, for a deficit of two percent or one percent by 2032.

    The idea is not new. Germany already has something similar, known as the debt brake. Spain or Italy also have constitutional provisions aimed at controlling public debt and deficits.

    In France, the proposal was already put forward under former president Nicolas Sarkozy. But it never made it through the final stage of the constitutional amendment process.

    Read more

    Listen: What do France’s centre-right candidates want for Europe?

    This time, however, the proposal could gather enough votes, notably with support from the far-right National Rally, which backs the principle of a golden rule.

    How does this compare with the EU’s own budgetary rules? Well, in principle, it’s quite similar. EU member states have been required to keep their public deficits below three percent of GDP since the Maastricht treaty.

    But the reality is that at least ten member states are currently failing to meet that target. When a country breaks the rules, the commission can sound the alarm and ask the country concerned to present a plan to bring its deficit down, with a clear timeline.

    But governments are given time to get their finances back on track. There are several stages in the procedure before sanctions can eventually be imposed by the commission and the council.

    And, in practice, no EU country has ever had to pay a fine for persistently running an excessive budget deficit.

    A constitutional golden rule would be different. If the requirement is written into a country’s constitution, failing to comply could become a constitutional issue. Provided the constitutional court enforces it, that would create a much more direct legal obligation.

    So, which EU countries are actually keeping their deficits below the three percent threshold? There are 14 of them, so slightly more than half of the 27 member states.

    Read more

    Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down

    But five countries are doing more than simply staying below the limit: they are actually running a budget surplus. That means their governments are collecting more in revenue than they spend.

    Those five countries are Greece, Cyprus, Ireland, Portugal, and Denmark.

    Cyprus is particularly striking, with a budget surplus of more than three percent of GDP. That’s a very different picture from France, whose deficit is close to tive percent, or than Poland where the deficit hits seven percent.

    So, what’s Cyprus’s secret? Its economy is heavily geared towards tourism, financial services and maritime transport. Combined with controlled public spending, this has helped the country maintain economic growth over several years.

    Of course, that doesn’t mean Cyprus has always had such healthy public finances, or that the situation will necessarily last.

    And there’s another side to the story. Whether we’re talking about Cyprus, Greece or Germany, keeping public finances under tight control often means limiting increases in public spending.

    And that can mean public services struggling to meet people’s needs, particularly in hospitals and schools.

    Austerity is increasingly becoming a political issue across Europe. And even in countries with relatively healthy public finances, citizens are feeling the pressure as their purchasing power continues to come under strain.

    Because ultimately, balancing the books doesn’t necessarily mean that people’s living standards are improving.

    The way Ukrainians have expanded the scope of the naval war has now alarmed the Russians, who are calling for the same kind of retaliation. It is highly likely that the seas around Europe will cease to be safe for Russian and Ukrainian ships in the long term.

    The Russians felt this particularly painfully off the Libyan coast at Benghazi on Saturday. One of the Russian navy’s most modern ships, the Merkur corvette, was moored at the port quay. Its destruction demonstrates the Ukrainian army’s expanding capabilities to weaken Russian influence around the world not through sabotage, but through direct military operations.

    The Merkur corvette was one of five Project 20380-class ships.

Should streets named after Pushkin be renamed? Where do we draw the line between rejecting Russian imperialism and preserving Russian cultural heritage? These are some of the questions director general of the Ukrainian Institute Volodymyr Sheiko discusses with EUobserver. ]]> Far from the Ukrainian front, Russia continues to enjoy a privileged place in European public life. In schools, museums and cultural institutions, Europeans encounter its renowned writers, artists and historical figures – Tolstoy, Pushkin, Soviet general Ivan Konev … and many others.

    Yet something that might seem distant from the realities of war, something as abstract as art and culture, is in reality another front in this conflict.

    As Ukraine fights for its very existence, it is also fighting over its identity: how it sees itself, how it defines its history, and how it understands the identity of its enemy – Russia.

    Should Russian cultural figures continue to be celebrated in European public spaces? Should streets named after Pushkin be renamed? Where do we draw the line between rejecting Russian imperialism and preserving Russian cultural heritage? These are some of the questions director general of the Ukrainian Institute Volodymyr Sheiko discusses in the following interview.

    Russian culture is frequently used in public discourse. Suppose the leader of a major EU country began a speech with the line, “Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way”, the opening sentence of Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina. Would that be problematic for you?

    It would trouble me, yes. Not because I believe Tolstoy should never be quoted, but because we need to ask what that quotation is doing at this particular moment.

    When an EU leader opens a major speech with Tolstoy while Russia is bombing Ukrainian cities, the choice is not entirely neutral. It reinforces the idea that Russian culture is still the natural source of universal wisdom, something every European is expected to recognise and admire.

    And I think we need to question that reflex. For generations, Russian culture was presented as universal, while Ukrainian, Georgian or Crimean Tatar cultures were treated as regional or secondary. Russia was the centre; everyone else was the periphery.

    So, my first response would be: why Tolstoy? Why not Lesia Ukrainka? Her Cassandra, a masterpiece of literary modernism, is about someone who understands the truth but cannot persuade others to act before catastrophe arrives. That seems painfully relevant to European politics today. The work is now available in a contemporary English translation and is increasingly recognised for its treatment of political blindness, colonial subjugation and the isolation of the person who voices an inconvenient truth. 

    Or take Taras Shevchenko’s words, “Fight, and you will prevail.” Or Ivan Franko’s Moses, with its vision of Ukraine taking its place among the world’s free nations, “in your own house, in your own fields’ broad spaces”. A politician could also invoke Mykola Khvylovy’s call to turn “away from Moscow” and towards a confident European cultural future. These references are no less powerful or universal. Europeans simply don’t know these amazing writers.

    So, I am not calling for Tolstoy to disappear from libraries. I am asking why a Russian writer still comes to mind so automatically when a European leader wants to say something profound about the human condition.

    A political speech is not a literature seminar. It tells us whose words and experiences Europe places at the centre. At a time when Russia is trying to destroy Ukraine as a distinct culture and political nation, European leaders should be especially aware of that choice.

    Are literature and art exempt from war, or are they part of the soft power used by an aggressor state?

    My short answer is that there is nothing soft about Russian soft power.

    We usually think of soft power as attraction: a country presents its culture and values and hopes others will find them appealing. Russia’s cultural power has often worked in a much harder way. It tells the world that Ukrainian language, history and culture are not fully separate, that Ukraine belongs naturally within a Russian cultural space, and that Russia has a special right to speak for our entire region. Such mindset prepares the ground for political control and military invasion.

    You can see it in museums that have described Ukrainian artists as ‘Russian’, in universities where “Eastern European studies” effectively meant Russian studies, or in international media that continued to use Russian versions of Ukrainian toponyms. Each example may seem small. Together, they create a mental map in which Russia is the centre and its neighbours are merely its extensions.

    Read more

    Russian attack against Kyiv’s holiest monastery shows Kremlin’s desire to wipe out Ukraine heritage, says theologian

    The full-scale invasion made that connection impossible to ignore. Russia is destroying hundreds of museums, archives, theatres and historic buildings in Ukraine. In the occupied territories, it removes and burns Ukrainian books, suppresses Ukrainian education and rewrites local history. The military violence follows the cultural claim: if Ukraine is not a real nation, then its sovereignty can be treated as a collateral accident.

    Russia tries to occupy the imagination before it occupies the territory. That is why I would not describe its cultural influence as “soft”.

    At the same time, I do not want Ukraine to respond by turning its own culture into propaganda. Ukrainian literature, music, cinema and art matter because they are strong, independent and diverse, not because they illustrate a government message or the latest news from the front.

      <title>Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/jensen-huang-nvidia-apologizes-staff</link>
      <description><p>Huang acknowledges he violated code of conduct by having affairs, but denied Trump was instrumental in his return</p><p>Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he’s caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.</p><p>“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/technology/jensen-huang-apology-nvidia-ceo.html">reviewed by the New York Times</a>. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/jensen-huang-nvidia-apologizes-staff">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/nov/24/school-bus-driver-decline-budget</link>
      <description><p>Total number of drivers dropped 5% over the last year and fell 15% compared with 2019 levels, new report finds</p><p>The number of school bus drivers in the US has dropped 5% over the last year as drivers continue to experience low pay, poor working conditions and school budget shortfalls, according to a new report.</p><p>The total number of school bus drivers is down 15%, or nearly 34,000 drivers, compared with 2019 levels, according to an new <a href="https://www.epi.org/blog/the-school-bus-driver-shortage-is-worsening-as-wages-fall-once-again/#_ref2">analysis</a> from the Economic Policy Institute.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/nov/24/school-bus-driver-decline-budget">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Sell-off signals investors are bracing for further volatility in key AI sector driving economic growth worldwide</p><p>Technology shares led a market retreat Tuesday as caution returned after Jensen Huang’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/mistake-corrected-jensen-huang-resinstated-nvidia-analysis">extraordinary return</a> to Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide.</p><p>A day after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO drove Nvidia shares up more than 30%, adding more than $900bn to the firm’s market value, the euphoria dissipated as its stock lost almost 6% by Tuesday’s close.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/24/nvidia-stock-falls-jensen-huang">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer</link>
      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 25 Nov 2026 05:13:59 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Tullow Oil shares rally after settling $387m tax disputes with Ghana]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/tullow-oil-shares-rally-after-settling-387m-tax-disputes-with-ghana/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/tullow-oil-shares-rally-after-settling-387m-tax-disputes-with-ghana/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 18:15:42 +0000Tullow Oil shares rallied strongly in London on Tuesday as the explorer reached a deal with Ghana on how to resolve two tax disputes totalling $387 million (€353 million), plus penalties, easing the path for the company to progress refinancing plans and continue to invest in key oilfields off the country’s coast.

The International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) ruled in September that Ghana was entitled to collect $196.5 million of tax the country argued it was owed on business interruption insurance payments Tullow received between 2016 and 2019. Ghana has also said a penalty equal to 100 per cent of the amount was also owed.

The Irish-founded company was also facing a separate tribunal hearing next year over a $190.5 million loan-interest tax dispute with Ghana. The African country has also claimed a right to a 100 per cent penalty in that case.

Tullow said on Tuesday that it has reached a payment deal with Ghana – estimated to be worth as much as $537.5 million – that would resolve both cases.

Shares in Tullow soared more than 20 per cent in London, but are still trading at less than half the level they were changing hands at before the ICC ruling in September.

“We are pleased to have come to an arrangement with the government of Ghana to resolve the outstanding liabilities related to the two tax arbitrations,” said Ian Perks, chief executive of Tullow Oil.

“This agreement, subject to approval by parliament, will enable Tullow to continue with its refinancing plans which are progressing and will support ongoing investment in the Jubilee and TEN developments which are nationally important assets.”

The heavily-indebted company has refocused its business primarily on its core Jubilee and TEN oilfields off the coast of Ghana, following the completion in 2025 of the sales of its assets in Gabon and Kenya as part of a wider programme to dispose of noncore assets and strengthen its balance sheet.

Tullow loss widens as refinancing and tax costs outweigh oil price spike

The accord with the Ghanaian government includes a $112 million upfront payment and the transfer to the government of about $91 million in receivables due to the company. Further cash payments of $40 million next year and $44.5 million in 2028 can be deferred if oil prices are below $90 a barrel.

It will also grant Ghana revenues from 100 billion cubic feet of gas produced at the Jubilee field from 2029, which is reported to be worth more than $250 million.

Tullow agreed a major refinancing in April that saw $1.3 billion of bonds that was due in May replaced by bonds and loans that start to mature from 2028. The deal was accepted by 99 per cent of bondholders and Glencore, a commodities trading firm that is a lender to the company.

The company is now working on refinancing plans ahead of borrowings starting to mature in 2028.

Tullow was founded by Irishman Aidan Heavey in 1985 in Tullow, Co Carlow. It moved its domicile to the UK more than two decades ago, closed its Dublin office in 2020 and delisted from the Dublin stock market in 2022.

]]><![CDATA[European shares fall as tech rally fades despite Jensen Huang jolt]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/european-shares-fall-as-tech-rally-fades-after-jensen-huang-jolt/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/european-shares-fall-as-tech-rally-fades-after-jensen-huang-jolt/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 18:41:09 +0000European shares closed lower on Tuesday after their strongest session in six months as a technology-led rebound lost momentum.

European technology stocks had risen more than 4 per cent on Monday in their biggest one-day jump ​since early April, after Jensen Huang’s surprise reinstatement as chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia boosted global risk appetite for the sector.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 edged down 0.7 per cent at 632.77 points on Tuesday.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index closed 1.5 per cent lower at 14,421.15. Banking stocks were out of sorts, with AIB falling 2.9 per cent to €10.97 and Bank of Ireland slipping 2 per cent to €18.42 – in line with a sell-off by sector players in the UK.

Kingspan was another weak spot among large companies, falling 4.1 per cent to €90.25.

Bucking the trend, Kerry Group advanced 1.8 per cent to €103.70.

London

Of Irish interest, Tullow Oil closed 15 per cent higher as the explorer reached a deal with Ghana on how to resolve two tax disputes totalling $387 million (€353 million), plus penalties, easing the path for the company to progress refinancing plans and continue to invest in key oilfields off the country’s coast.

The FTSE 100 index ended down 0.1 per cent. Mining shares were among the biggest weights on the index as copper ⁠and gold prices retreated, with Antofagasta dropping 8.1 per cent, Anglo American off 5.7 per cent ‌and Glencore ‌losing ​4.8 per cent.

Banks were also among the top drags, with HSBC Holdings down 2.7 per cent and Barclays falling 2.5 per cent.

Among defensive stocks, ​Unilever rose 2 per cent, GSK gained 2.5 per cent and ​AstraZeneca added 2.9 per cent.

Among others, caterer Compass Group gained about 4.2 per cent after reporting fiscal 2026 organic revenue growth above analysts’ expectations and reaffirming plans ‌to shift its primary listing to New York.

Home improvement retailer Kingfisher, owner of B&Q, ​slipped 4.8 per cent as weaker trading in France and Poland overshadowed a modest profit forecast upgrade.

Europe

Aixtron retreated 16.3 per cent, unwinding part of the previous session’s gains, after UBS downgraded the chip systems manufacturer to sell. Peers Infineon and ASM International dropped more than 9 per cent and 8 per cent, respectively.

In Europe, miners were the biggest percentage losers, down almost 5 per cent as prices of gold and copper slipped.

Sanofi gained 9.7 per cent to top the Stoxx 600 after the pharma company said it would acquire US drugmaker Insmed for $41 billion, marking the largest acquisition of chief executive Belén Garijo’s tenure.

The announcement boosted healthcare stocks, up nearly ‌2 per cent.

New York

The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 were lower in early-afternoon trading as investors retreated from artificial intelligence (AI)-linked shares after an Nvidia-fuelled rally. They were also awaiting inflation data before the Federal Reserve’s ​December meeting.

The pullback followed outsize gains on Monday, when Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive. Nvidia shares surged 31.5 per cent in that session, adding nearly $1 trillion (€910 billion) to the company’s market value.

On Tuesday, the stock fell as investors weighed the implications of Huang’s reinstatement, focusing on the political and governance risks surrounding his return.

Other chip stocks followed suit.

Neocloud companies also gave back some of Monday’s gains, with CoreWeave and Nebius ⁠down sharply.

Before Monday’s rebound, AI-linked stocks had ​struggled for weeks as investors questioned the sector’s debt-fuelled spending and the returns ​it could generate.

Anthropic’s shares tumbled to $76, well below their $83 initial public offering price last week, as the AI start-up’s blockbuster market debut last week failed to rekindle enthusiasm ‌for the AI trade.

Amazon and Alphabet, two of ​Anthropic’s biggest investors, were each down.

A Conference Board survey showed US consumer confidence rose to its highest level in nearly two years in November amid optimism over the labour market and the economy following this month’s midterm elections.

Traders are fully pricing in a quarter of a percentage point US Federal Reserve rate hike next month and see a slim chance of a 0.5 of a point move, up from zero a day earlier, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]><![CDATA[Tech company Tines posts pretax loss of €33m, but revenue also up as products make a mark]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/tech-company-tines-posts-pretax-loss-of-33m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/tech-company-tines-posts-pretax-loss-of-33m/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 19:03:07 +0000Irish tech company Tines recorded a pretax loss of almost $36 million (€33 million), widening from $24.9 million in the previous year due to heavy investment.

The company saw revenues rise significantly as its products continued to gain traction in the market.

Founded by Eoin Hinchy and Thomas Kinsella in 2018, Tines developed a workflow and artificial intelligence (AI) platform to help businesses operate more efficiently and mitigate risks.

Accounts filed for the company for the year ending January 31st, 2026, showed Tines’ revenue from contracts with customers rose more than two-thirds to $66.2 million over the period.

The bulk of that comes from its customers in the US, which is the company’s primary market, and accounted for more than $50 million.

Cost of sales doubled over the period to almost $15.6 million, while distribution costs and other administrative costs also rose sharply. That included staff costs, with wages and salaries increasing to $66.95 million, up from $43 million in 2025.

Gross profit was $50.7 million, up from $31.7 million in 2025. Operating losses widened to $43.7 million, from $27.5 million in the previous year.

Tines raised $125 million last year in a Series C round that gave it a valuation of more than $1 billion. That funding has helped to bolster research spending, which totalled $2.2 million in the year to the end of January 2026, up from $1.4 million in 2025.

Tines has been investing heavily in AI product development, shipping new generative AI features and agentic capabilities, and launching a new platform in July called Tines 3B.

“Fundamentally, the shift in technology allowed us to take everything we know and ask, ‘what would the product look like if we were building it today with everything we have at our disposal?’,” said Niall Cowman, Tines’ vice president of finance. “Tines 3B is a vastly different experience for non-technical people like myself to be able to build and create in a secure environment.”

It has also been expanding its workforce. Tines employed 325 people during the year, up almost 50 per cent from the 220 it employed in 2025.

The company said last month it would create 100 jobs in Ireland over the next two years across its product, engineering, sales, customer success, marketing and operations teams, earmarking more than half of the roles for new entrants to the jobs market.

It has also been expanding its business in other regions such as Asia Pacific.

“With this funding round we were able to say let’s carve out and invest in these other regions because the demand is there,” Cowman said. “We just need to go out there and grab it.”

The company is also still aiming to reach $100 million in revenues, with Cowman confident that it will reach the milestone in the current fiscal period.

]]><![CDATA[Entrepreneur Aimee Connolly receives €750,000 dividend from beauty brand]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/entrepreneur-aimee-connolly-receives-750000-dividend-from-beauty-brand/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/entrepreneur-aimee-connolly-receives-750000-dividend-from-beauty-brand/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:03:33 +0000Irish entrepreneur Aimee Connolly paid herself a first dividend last year, of €750,000, after her beauty brand posted another year of strong growth in revenues and profits.

Latest accounts for Sculpted by Aimee Connolly Cosmetics Ltd, which were approved on November 16th, show its revenues rose by 18 per cent to €38.4 million. Its pretax profits increased by 7 per cent to €4.18 million.

The results were “considered satisfactory by the directors, who expect continued growth in the foreseeable future”.

In a post balance sheet event on January 22nd, 2026, the directors approved an interim dividend of €750,000 to Connolly’s SBACC Holdings Limited.

At the start of 2025, the company transferred its UK retail business to Sculpted by Aimee (UK) Limited as part of an internal group reorganisation.

The transfer comprised inventory, tangible fixed assets, the associated workforce and related working capital balances.

The number of staff employed by the Irish company increased from 91 to 111 last year. Staff costs rose from €4.46 million to €5.68 million.

Staff participate in a group share option scheme operated by its parent entity. A charge of €87,891 relating to the options is recognised in the accounts.

Connolly established her cosmetics business in 2016 after she saved up €10,000 by working as a freelance make-up artist.

The business mixes bricks and mortar stores – it has outlets on Grafton Street, Dublin, at Kildare Village, on Carnaby Street, London, and in Victoria Square, Belfast – and a thriving SculptedbyAimee.com ecommerce business.

In an interview with The Irish Times in April, Connolly set out her ambitions for the brand over the next decade. “The goal is to be in the top 10 beauty brands globally in the next decade. It’s a huge goal and it’s a big mountain to climb, but I have never felt more passionate to do so,” she said.

Directors’ remuneration last year totalled €918,546, comprising pay of €648,546 and pension contributions of €270,000.

The company recorded an operating profit of €4.44 million. Interest payments of €253,903 left it with a pretax profit of just under €4.2 million.

A corporation tax charge of €518,357 reduced its after-tax profit to €3.66 million.

The strong performance in 2025 strengthened the Sculpted by Aimee company’s balance sheet, where accumulated profits totalled €16.23 million at the end of last year. Cash funds increased from €6.5 million to €8.07 million.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Shop worker who said boss tried to extort her of inheritance wins unfair dismissal case]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/shop-worker-who-said-businessman-tried-to-extort-her-of-inheritance-wins-dismissal-case/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/shop-worker-who-said-businessman-tried-to-extort-her-of-inheritance-wins-dismissal-case/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:14:23 +0000A shop worker has told the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) she left her dying mother’s bedside for a meeting with her boss, where he attempted to “extort” €10,000 from her before forcing her to resign. The employee, Louise McManus, has won her unfair dismissal case.

McManus said Dublin businessman Colm Beattie “falsely” told gardaí she had stolen from him. He made the allegations, McManus said, following her decision to bring a case to the employment tribunal. She said his complaints to gardaí led to her arrest.

“To be put in a cell for doing nothing wrong, it takes its toll on you,” the worker told a hearing earlier this year.

She said she wanted Beattie, the company director, with an address at Castlewood, Rathmines, Dublin 6, “named and shamed” in preference to compensation.

McManus has now been awarded €9,010 for multiple employment rights breaches in a WRC ruling against Beattie’s firm, Branstock Retail Ltd, which employed eight people at a Spar shop on Errigal Road in Drimnagh, Dublin 12. She worked in the shop from January 2022 to May 2025.

McManus told a hearing in March that Beattie initially paid her the minimum wage by bank transfer, but later promoted her to assistant manager and augmented her pay with a €70 cash top-up every Sunday – a sum she collected from a safe on the premises.

In March 2024, her mother was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer, she said. Beattie told her the business could not pay her, so she agreed to cut her hours to a three-day week.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[The economics of the AI boom are actually quite old-fashioned]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000This week saw the largest share offering the world has ever seen. Anthropic, the AI company that makes Claude, floated on the US stock market with an initial value of just over $1 trillion – a thousand billion dollars. Founded only six years ago, it is today the 10th most valuable corporation in the US.

With the share offering coming a week after the Jensen Huang scandal, it seems that the world is captured by some AI story or another. Even global politics is in thrall to this new technology. On Thursday, when Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat together, it was clear that the new cold war was as much about tech as arms. We are looking at an industrial transformation on the scale of the move to oil and gas in the early 20th century. It will change the world, but that doesn’t mean everyone can profit from it.

Despite all the money flooding into what is known as “the AI trade”, there seems to be precious little understanding of the economics underpinning the AI boom. Where is the money going, why is everything so expensive and what are the risks that it collapses following one big speculative mania?

When so few people have the answers, it makes sense to ask the questions.

The AI story is portrayed as a high-end technology story, but when you drill down a bit, the economics of AI seem close to old-fashioned heavy industry. It involves pouring concrete, connecting power grids and buying manufactured microchips at a large scale. The lion’s share of the money goes on imported hardware. Very little of the spending is creating new tech jobs. And a growing share of the AI buildout – estimated to be $1 trillion this year – is being financed with borrowings that will need to be paid back sooner or later.

Who is profiting at the moment, who is paying, and how long can it last?

Most of the profits are being made by chipmakers largely based in Asia. Most of the cost is borne by the companies in the US doing all the borrowing, those building or renting the data centres. In addition, as almost everything uses chips – your phone, your car and your fridge – we are all paying through higher costs in our data-driven economy. The amount of new debt means the AI boom is dependent on the rate of interest, the patience of lenders and the tolerance of local communities for data centres, which were a big issue in the US midterms, as was a general dislike of the tech titans who dominate the AI world.

A data centre needs four things: chips, land, water and electricity. Building a new facility can take about two years. There’s a lot of concrete to pour. The amount of money, water and electricity required is enormous. Consider a 1 gigawatt (GW) campus of data centres. Granted, this is a huge data centre but it gives us an idea of the scale of the industrial transformation in front of us. One GW of electricity roughly corresponds to the output of a nuclear power plant or the annual electricity for some 650,000 houses – bigger than Dublin. About 10.5 billion gallons of water are needed to cool the machines, about enough for 100,000 households, and it needs around 700-1,100 acres of space, about half the total size of Phoenix Park. Are you beginning to grasp the scale?

There is little indication we have a plan for what to do if the AI bubble bursts

Most data centres are not this big, running on the megawatt rather than gigawatt scale, closer to 100-250MW of energy, but the demands of AI mean this figure is trending relentlessly upwards, which makes it worthwhile to look at the jumbo data centre.

A 1GW data centre costs about $50 billion – roughly $15 billion for the facility and $35 billion for the compute to power it. Chips make up roughly 70 per cent of the total cost. Because chips dominate the cost, the profits flow to whoever makes them. Nvidia and the amorous Jensen Huang may well design these chips, but they do not manufacture them. Rather, the likes of SK Hynix, TSMC and others do, with Korea, Taiwan and Japan controlling manufacturing. Others will want to get in on the game.

AI fever is producing some strange symptoms

The hyperscalers, companies such as Google and Meta, are designing their own chips, elbowing in on Nvidia’s turf. Geo-strategically, rival suppliers, particularly in China, will emerge. Greater supply of chips will bring down the cost and as the cost of chips falls, the price of using AI will fall. The dilemma for companies such as Anthropic is that if the price of using it falls, its revenues will fall, undermining its new position as the 10th most valuable company in the US.

Not only is the industrial model changing rapidly, with new competitors emerging at every stage of the supply chain, but maybe – more critically – the financing of the AI transformation has changed from cash flow to debt and equity. The hyperscalers, such as Google, used to finance their AI businesses from their large cash flow but, as the costs have risen, even a big company such as Google has had to start borrowing money.

About 10 per cent of all global investment-grade bonds are already related to AI, possibly rising to 16–19 per cent by next year. The AI borrower is in a highly competitive market. For example, the US government bond yields roughly 5 per cent with essentially no risk, so every data centre bond competes with sovereign debt.

Moreover, central banks that are trying to bear down on inflation are raising interest rates, pushing up rates everywhere. Markets are already getting nervous. Hyperscalers with other subscription businesses can borrow cheaply, but others such as Oracle are paying the widest spread. There is also another group of AI-related businesses called neo-clouds that offer cheaper data centre services than Google, Meta, Amazon or Microsoft. You might have heard of names such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe. They are paying much higher interest to get money and are most exposed to any change in interest rates or market sentiment.

Over the past few weeks, the huge amounts of money involved have put the wind up financial markets. Can the AI companies such as Anthropic that have yet to make a profit generate money to validate their huge valuations? Will the hyperscalers continue to bankroll our datacentres? Will banks start to call in loans? And can all this credit continue to flow into a sector that is spending so much but – at least so far – is earning so little?

We’ve seen boom and bust before. Will this be the biggest one?

]]>imaginima<![CDATA[Tax-free lump-sum loophole for workers is set to close in Finance Act]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/24/tax-free-lump-sum-loophole-set-to-close-in-finance-act/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/24/tax-free-lump-sum-loophole-set-to-close-in-finance-act/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 05:28:00 +0000It has long been the case that workers can benefit from a tax-free lump sum of up to €200,000 throughout their lifetime, and across redundancy payouts and various pension vehicles.

However, a loophole has been in place, which meant some people, either inadvertently or deliberately, have been able to benefit from the tax advantages during both redundancy and retirement.

Now the Government is working on closing this mismatch in the upcoming Finance Act. What will it mean for tax-free lump sums going forward? And how should people plan for a lump sum at retirement?

Finance Bill update

The tax-free lump sum does not have to be received just the once, it can be paid out several times – in a termination payment, different pension pots, etc – but they must reference each other up to the limit of €200,000.

If you opt to avail of it (or some of it) in a termination payment, then you must sign a waiver indicating that you have already availed of it.

However, this waiver is only tied to that current employment – and so if someone was to leave a job, use the lump sum to reduce the amount of tax payable on their redundancy payment, and transfer their pension to a PRSA, then they could once more avail of the lump sum at retirement, because they would no longer be claiming in relation to that old employment, as PRSAs aren’t covered by the waiver.

This situation has been in place since 2002, when PRSAs were created.

“As a result you had a slightly unusual result whereby occupational pension schemes were included when you were calculating pension lump sums that one might receive. But PRSAs were excluded,” says Munro O’Dwyer, a partner with PwC.

It may not have been a big cohort that availed of it. First of all, you would have had to receive a termination payment and the figures would need to have been substantial enough to make use of possible double lump sum.

And many may not realise the impact of having some pension funds in a PRSA.

“People who had previously waived their right to a pension lump sum have inadvertently benefited from this loophole,” says Jim Connolly, head of pensions with Goodbody.

But it’s likely that others may have deliberately availed of it.

“Where it gets a lot more grey is where people took an action to position themselves in PRSAs, to take advantage of this mismatch,” says O’Dwyer.

Given the mismatch – and the possibility for people to avail of it in excess of the lifetime limit – in this year’s Finance Bill there has been a move to close this, by extending the waiver to “the broader suite of modern pension products that are now available”. These include PRSAs, MyFutureFund, pan-European pension products, as well as foreign pension plans.

In that way, the tax relief on offer should be the same to all – regardless of the pension product in place.

Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?

It is expected that the change will take place from January 1st, 2027, pending enactment of the Finance Bill. So, if you’re calculating something from January 1st, 2027, O’Dwyer says PRSAs will be in scope.

“What’s less clear is for waivers signed historically,” he says.

But the Finance Bill may yet be changed before it is enacted.

How is my lump sum calculated?

If you haven’t accessed some of your lump sum in a redundancy payment – or at least did so prior to the Finance Bill amendment – the maximum tax-free amount at retirement depends on one of two calculations.

Firstly, if it’s a PRSA, it will always be based on 25 per cent of the fund, up to €200,000. A retirement fund of €100,000 would mean a tax-free lump sum of €25,000; a €300,000 fund would mean a tax-free lump sum of €75,000; a €500,000 fund would get €125,000; and €1 million, €200,000 (plus €50,000 to be taxed).

A favourable rate of tax, at 20 per cent, applies on the next tranche of between €200,000 and €500,000. Above that you’ll face your marginal rate of tax. The balance of the fund can then be put into either an annuity or an approved retirement fund (ARF).

This rule also applies to occupational schemes, but there is another way of calculating the tax-free element: the salary and service formula. This depends on how long you’ve worked with your current employer, and your final pensionable salary. If you are eligible this can be 1.5 times your final salary – so can exceed the other calculation. Someone with a pension fund of €150,000 for example, would get only €37,500 based on the 25 per cent calculation but could get the full amount if they had a salary of €100,000.

But it’s not just about how much you earn when you retire, according to Connolly. Revenue applies a “final remuneration” approach to calculating this figure, which means that you can look back over salary history up to 10 years – and take the best average.

The kicker with the salary and service calculation, however, is that you have to buy an annuity with your fund (apart from your additional voluntary contributions or AVCs as they are better known).

If you have a bumper pension pot, and will easily meet the €200,000 tax-free limit, then how you calculate this lump sum won’t matter. What’s more of a concern is how you draw down your pension income via an ARF or annuity.

“For a higher earner it’s not going to cause much of a complication,” says O’Dwyer.

If, however, your fund won’t hit the limit then it needs more attention.

“If you’ve a million euro in your fund – it’s simple, you get €200,000. The challenge is if you’ve €150,000,” says O’Dwyer, noting that someone might want to maximise their tax-free amount via a salary and service calculation – but may not want to buy an annuity.

Pension millionaires to benefit from higher tax relief over coming years

There could be an argument then, to remove the annuity requirement from the salary and service option.

“In some respect, having different options is fine, but prescribing what you do with the balance is where the issue comes in,” O’Dwyer says.

What if I’m in a defined-benefit pension scheme?

According to Connolly, lump-sum planning for those in defined-benefit (DB) schemes can be tricky, as to take a tax-free lump-sum of 1.5 times final salary will reduce the pension payments. This is known as commutation. Those with such a pension plan also have an option of taking 25 per cent of the pension fund if they get a transfer value and move the fund.

But those in DB plans don’t always have the full information to make the best decision. “Trustees generally don’t make them aware they have the option of a transfer value,” says Connolly, noting there can be a “massive difference” between the two ways of calculating the lump sum.

Moreover, someone with a serious illness, for example, may be better to get the transfer value, rather than have their pension paid out in an annuity.

While there is no regulatory requirement to offer a retiree a transfer value, Connolly argues there is a fiduciary one to act in the best interest of members of the DB scheme.

“I would have an eye on my lump-sum entitlements from age 50 onwards,” says Connolly.

The age 50 is a pertinent one, as this is the age you may be able to access certain pension pots, such as those from older employments – you don’t have to draw down all your pots at the same time.

“You can have as many retirements as you’ve had jobs,” says Connolly, and you can take 25 per cent each time you draw a pot down – up to the lifetime limit of €200,000.

But there is a complication. If you use salary and service to calculate your lump sum, and only have 20 years’ service, you’ll need to use the uplift approach to get 1.5 times final salary.

But this enhanced scale means “you do have to reference retained benefits” from other pension pots, O’Dwyer says.

In February 2025 the White House barred the Associated Press (AP) from the Oval Office and Air Force One because its stylebook continued to refer to the Gulf of Mexico.

The AP was hardly alone. The New York Times, the BBC and the Guardian never adopted Gulf of America either. But the venerable wire service is the default rule book for most American local newspapers, broadcasters and press offices. Change one AP entry and thousands of publications follow. In fact it is the nearest thing the English-speaking world has to the academies that police the language in France or Spain.

English is famously protean and mutable. Many see that as the reason for its global dominance (along with a spot of imperialism, of course). That has not stopped people trying to bend it for political ends.

Trump’s efforts may be unusually crude but they are far from unprecedented, and media organisations regularly have to decide whether to go along or hold the line.

Take the AP’s own decision in June 2020, weeks after the murder of George Floyd, to capitalise “Black”. The argument was that the word denoted a shared history and identity, particularly among Americans whose enslaved ancestors had been cut off from any national origin.

“White” stayed lower case, supposedly because it described no comparable culture and because white supremacists liked the capital. Many, including the National Association of Black Journalists, found that asymmetry hard to justify.

Still, the change swept American media, including Fox News and the Wall Street Journal. It travelled less well across the Atlantic, where it remains largely lower case, or inconsistent, in Irish and British media. And the Irish writer Emma Dabiri has argued against the capital letter altogether, on the grounds that it entrenches racial categories she regards as inventions of white supremacy.

Opinion polls are core to how media covers politics, but is that a good thing?

An even less successful innovation was “Latinx”, a gender-neutral alternative to Latino and Latina. It caught on in parts of academia and the media, but the AP only ever allowed it in quotes or for people who requested it, and barely one in 25 Hispanic Americans used it.

It became shorthand for woke excess, imposed by English-speaking language police on people who never asked for it.

Left and right do seem to approach these issues differently. Progressives have drawn on theories of language as an instrument of power and sought to reshape attitudes by reshaping vocabulary. The right’s approach, exemplified by the AI-to-SI switch, owes less to Michel Foucault than to Madison Avenue.

Two examples from half a century ago illustrate the point. In the early 1970s, opponents of abortion rebranded their movement as “pro-life”. It worked, up to a point, uniting supporters under a positive banner. But the term never shed its partisan charge, and most newsroom style guides, including those of the AP and The Irish Times, still avoid it.

Around the same time, Gloria Steinem launched Ms magazine. The honorific dated from 1901, but the activist Sheila Michaels revived it on New York radio in 1969. The New York Times held out until 1986. Ms is now the unremarkable default on forms and in correspondence, because it solved a practical problem people of every political stripe recognised.

Latinx may be in retreat, but de-gendering remains a live battle in languages where gender is built into nouns and adjectives. The French Senate voted in 2023 to outlaw gender-neutral “écriture inclusive” in official documents. Bavaria and Germany’s federal government have restricted gender asterisks. Sweden, by contrast, added the neutral pronoun “hen” to its official glossary in 2015, and about half the population now uses it.

For editors in the English-speaking world, the lesson is that the words that last are the useful ones. Fashionable theories and rebranding campaigns will always come second to how people actually choose to speak. Super intelligence seems doomed already, given that Markwayne Mullin himself couldn’t even keep it up for the whole press conference.

]]><![CDATA[I’ve done some sums and concluded many AI investors could lose their shirts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/23/john-fitzgerald-ive-done-some-sums-and-concluded-many-ai-investors-could-lose-their-shirts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/23/john-fitzgerald-ive-done-some-sums-and-concluded-many-ai-investors-could-lose-their-shirts/Mon, 23 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Artificial intelligence (AI) is already affecting global economies, but the likely long-term beneficial impact is hard to quantify. What we are seeing at this early stage is the danger that AI can go rogue. Europe is, rightly, focusing on how to regulate this technology so that it benefits rather than harms society.

Massive AI investment is driving the US’s growth figures. The UK National Institute for Economic and Social Research (NIESR) estimates that investment in data centres will add 1.2 per cent to US GDP in 2028. This spending will also have a noticeable effect on growth in other economies supplying AI inputs, such as Mexico and Taiwan.

NIESR expects that this higher growth will have a small positive effect on UK exports. However, that benefit will be offset by the impact of higher interest rates due to the AI boom and its related inflationary stimulus.

The cost of government debt, in both the US and Europe, has also risen due to the scale of borrowing by tech companies to fund AI investments. Higher interest rates are squeezing other capital investment, such as housing. While these effects are particularly acute in the US, they are also impacting on Europe.

At the current rate of investment in AI, over the next five or six years it will cumulatively amount to a quarter of US GDP. A lot of this is spent on importing computer chips and electrical equipment for data centres. The pace of spending has led to huge inflation in the cost of such equipment, with knock-on effects worldwide on the cost of electricity generation and transmission.

US voters have rejected data centres and AI. What happens now?

There is a real concern that the AI investment boom could prove to be a bubble which will burst if it doesn’t prove profitable enough to pay its way.

While the buildings and electrical equipment are longer lasting, studies (including by our Central Bank) show that the chips, which are the biggest part of the cost of data centres, wear out or become obsolete after between three and six years. To get their money back, AI investors first need to cover the cost of these rapidly wasting assets.

To do this, by 2032 the AI sector would need revenue of about 3.5 per cent of US GDP. To cover their interest, energy and labour costs, and to get a return on their investment, the AI companies would need annual revenue of another 2.5 per cent of GDP, taking the total earnings required to 6 per cent of GDP.

Ireland is investing €19bn in upgrading our electricity system. Much of this will be needed anyway. However, there is a risk that we build too much capacity to serve data centres that could go out of business when the music stops

To hit that, other sectors of the economy would need to spend massive amounts buying AI technology. But that scale of spending on AI will only be justified if the resulting gains cover the outlay, either through major increases in productivity or significant cost savings.

For example, if all the savings were achieved through reduced payroll, it would mean a cut in US employment of more than 10 per cent, which won’t happen. And while labour productivity is rising, to date it is nowhere near enough to pay for all the investment in AI. Hence, the real possibility that many AI investors could lose their shirts.

What will happen to Ireland if the AI bubble bursts?

Of course US AI companies sell abroad, not just to the US market. But to get the required return on their investment, these companies would need every woman, man and child on the planet to buy more than €200 of AI services every year. This is not going to happen.

While AI does bring real benefits, the unbridled nature of the current AI race is a risk to the investors themselves and to the wider economy.

If and when the AI bubble bursts, the economic boom it has generated will go into reverse. The world will be left with more AI capacity and more data centres than it needs, and fewer new homes and other infrastructure than if other capital investments hadn’t been squeezed by the AI boom.

We in Ireland are not immune if the AI bubble bursts.

Ireland is investing €19 billion in upgrading our electricity system. Much of this will be needed anyway. However, there is a risk that we build too much capacity to serve data centres that could go out of business when the music stops.

To guard against the financial risk involved, data centres should be charged the full upfront cost of strengthening our electricity system, with an offset of lower charges over the following 20 years. This would avoid the danger that Ireland would be hurt if we were left with stranded electricity assets following any major disruption to the AI sector.

And it could also get personal. Because AI accounts for so much of the stock market, an AI bust would also affect pension funds across the developed world, including in Ireland.

Trump referred to his departure as “a tragedy” and called Huang a “brilliant man”. Elon Musk, head of SpaceX and Tesla, also rushed to Huang’s defence, describing him as “irreplaceable”.

For Alison Taylor, Huang’s story is a continuation of a baffling trend, one in which high-profile men get caught out having affairs with people either within their own company or with whom they do business.

“I’m not super judgmental – but just keep it out of your organisation,” she says. “Maybe don’t have an affair with your suppliers or your biggest customers or your competitors. Why can’t you go on a dating app and find somebody not connected to your business?

How to navigate the workplace relationship minefield

“What this all suggests is that there is a bigger problem with leadership. It feels like the people running these kinds of companies are surrounded by people who don’t say no – and they lose their sense of judgment”.

Tom Fox has a very straightforward piece of advice for high-ranking businessmen – as he says, it is nearly always men who are revealed as having affairs.

“I hate to sound like a complete prude,” he says, “but maybe being faithful to your wife is a good start.”
