Nvidia’s fall offers clues]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/23/was-jensen-huang-worth-570bn-nvidias-fall-offers-clues/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/23/was-jensen-huang-worth-570bn-nvidias-fall-offers-clues/Mon, 23 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000How much is Jensen Huang worth to Nvidia? About $570 billion, says economist Prof Tyler Cowen.

In a Free Press article, Cowen calls the former Nvidia boss an extreme example of his belief that, despite the “fulminating” about executive pay, many top chief executives are “significantly underpaid”.

Huang’s departure, he notes, coincided with a roughly $570 billion loss in Nvidia’s market value.

Indeed, shares have fallen further since Cowen’s calculation, despite a stellar earnings report that blew past analyst expectations. Additionally, since Huang’s departure also dragged down other AI stocks, Cowen suggests his contribution to the wider economy may have been even greater still.

There is an obvious qualification, namely that Nvidia’s share price decline cannot be treated as a straightforward measure of Huang’s value. His departure coincided with revelations about alleged misconduct, potential export-control violations, and possible legal consequences for the company.

Investors were digesting more than the loss of a chief executive. Still, it would be facile to pretend his departure has not unsettled Nvidia investors and the technology world in general.

Elon Musk compared Huang’s departure to kicking Michael Jordan off your team. Sequoia Capital’s Shaun Maguire declared him “irreplaceable”.

Former Goldman Sachs boss Lloyd Blankfein called it a “loss”, citing Huang’s “credibility, relationships and influence”. Andreessen Horowitz’s Martin Casado described it as a “dark, dark day”.

One Bernstein analyst put it succinctly: “Jensen is Nvidia.”

Chances of Jensen Huang making a Steve Jobs-like comeback go from slim to zero

However, while the best chief executives make themselves at least partially dispensable, adds Cowen, Huang did the opposite. About 60 people reported directly to him, concentrating enormous amounts of knowledge and authority in one person.

On earnings calls, he routinely fielded analysts’ questions himself. There is no obvious successor, as evidenced by prediction market Kalshi listing 37 possible candidates for Nvidia’s next permanent chief executive.

The aforementioned $570 billion is a measure of his extraordinary success, but also of the unnecessary risks he left behind.

There is, of course, another way of looking at all this. Blankfein was sad to see Huang go, describing it as “Shakespearean”. But, he added, quoting Charles de Gaulle, “The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.”

]]>Manuel Orbegozo<![CDATA[‘During Covid, we built a camper. The van is old but she is as strong as an ox’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/23/during-covid-we-built-a-camper-the-van-is-old-but-she-is-as-strong-as-an-ox/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/23/during-covid-we-built-a-camper-the-van-is-old-but-she-is-as-strong-as-an-ox/Mon, 23 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Broadcaster and presenter Marty Miller hosts Marty @ Work on Radio Nova between 10am and 1pm, Monday-Friday.

Are you a saver or a spender?

Sadly, I’m very much a spender. I tend to go nuts on most pay-days and then wonder why I’ve got nothing by the end of the month. Most frustratingly, I’m annoyed with myself for blasting through my income every month and counting down the days to the next cheque.

What was the first job you received money for, and how much were you paid?

I was a milk boy, and I loved it. I was a 10-year-old kid allowed out early to deliver milk on weekends. I was paid IR£21 at the time, and I was loaded. The financial independence I had from an early age was so great, and it makes me sad that kids can’t experience that kind of madness or responsibility any more.

Do you shop around for better value?

That depends on the item. From a car to a boiler to a turntable, I’ll research every bit of it before buying. But clothes and stuff, I don’t shop around. If I see something, and if I have the money, I’ll get it. Anything involving audio equipment is particularly dangerous. I can always find a reason why I “need” something new.

What has been your most extravagant purchase, and how much did it cost?

I suppose our camper van. During Covid, we built a camper. It’s fully winterised, very comfortable, and it’s completely our design. There wouldn’t be much change out of €40,000, but that’s nothing to spend on a camper. There is a lot of upkeep on it as she’s old, but she’s as strong as an ox.

‘It’s gone absolutely loony’: As Ireland’s campervan culture explodes, problems arise

What purchase have you made that you consider the best value for money?

The electric car and my motorcycle. Yes, the bike is getting dearer to fill, but it’s nothing like what some people spend on a forecourt. The electric car has been a game changer. The savings are astronomical.

Is there anything you regret spending money on?

Over the years, I’ve had a few classic VW Beetles, mostly late-1960s and early-1970s, but they always cost me more than I ever got for them.

Do you haggle over prices?

Not hugely, but I love Vinted and Done Deal, and will always offer less than the asking price. I suppose that is haggling. If they come back with a counter-offer, I don’t tend to engage. Take my offer, or don’t. I’ll find it somewhere else.

Radio Nova cracks into AI for ‘Mad Yolk’ advertising campaign

Do you invest in shares and/or cryptocurrency?

Crypto makes no sense to me. I have a tiny portfolio of stocks and shares, mostly in robotics and IT, but I keep it small. It ticks over and most seem to be going the right way.

Do you have a retirement or pension plan?

I have two. The state/employers’ thing that came into play last year [auto-enrolment] and my own one that I have had since I was 21. However, the latter portfolio has been wiped out numerous times because of various financial crashes. I’ve reduced it over the last year as life has just become too expensive.

What was the last thing you bought, and was it good value for money?

Recently, I bought an almost-new winter raincoat for the motorcycle. It cost me €25 on Vinted. It’s got all the padding in the back, shoulders and elbows and looks brand new. Great value for money.

Have you ever successfully saved up for a relatively big purchase?

The camper van. We paid for that after specifically saving for it. In 2009, my wife and I travelled to Australia, so a camper was always going to be in our future. Now we have it, thank goodness.

Have you ever lost money?

Yes, I have lost plenty, what with my pension wipeouts and the classic cars. As for the pension, the pot will be what it will be when I hit 66, so I don’t overthink it.

Are you a gambler and, if so, have you ever had a big win?

I am not. Zero interest. I don’t even play the lotto.

What is your best habit when it comes to money? And your worst?

The best is that I pay off all the bills, pay my pension and put a few quid into the shares accounts. The worst is that I can always find a way of convincing myself that another microphone, turntable or bit of kit is somehow a necessity. It’s a process to convince myself I don’t.

How much money do you have on you now?

Nothing cash-wise. I left cash behind me about eight years ago.

In conversation with Tony Clayton-Lea

   <description>Die Zahl der Toten im Ukraine-Krieg gilt auf beiden Seiten als Staatsgeheimnis. Poland and the United States have signed an agreement on defence research, development, testing and evaluation, concluding 17 years of negotiations and opening the way for deeper technological cooperation.

The agreement establishes a framework for joint defence projects, as well as the exchange of technical data and expertise, giving Poland – which is already a major importer of US arms – a formal role in the development of American defence technologies for the first time.

Under Secretary Emil Michael (@USWREMichael) and Mr. Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defence, signed the Agreement Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Poland for Defense Research,… pic.twitter.com/7EAgK3nD2i

— Department of War CTO (@DoWCTO) November 23, 2026

The agreement was signed at the Pentagon by Poland’s deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk and US under secretary of war for research and engineering Emil Michael.

According to the Department of War, the deal will help “turn research and development into validated military capabilities to jointly support US and Polish warfighters”.

Tomczyk said the agreement would allow Polish universities, research institutes and companies to participate in joint research and development work on defence technology with US partners and would enable such technologies to be tailored more closely to the requirements of the Polish armed forces.

During a briefing in Washington, Tomczyk admitted that the agreement had been negotiated for what he described as a “probably record-breaking” 17 years, but he noted a “significant acceleration in relations” between the US and Poland over the last six months.

 

General Marcin Górka, who oversees innovation in the Polish armed forces and accompanied Tomczyk to the United States, likewise welcomed the agreement, which he said would “open the doors to American military laboratories for our scientists and engineers”.

Górka also said the agreement would enable Poland and the United States to jointly develop anti-drone systems and advanced drones, with testing taking place in both countries.

Poland is a major importer of US military hardware. Between 2021 and 2025, it was the biggest overall importer of arms in NATO, with around 44% of that equipment coming from the US, including F-35 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence systems and HIMARS rocket launchers.

But Poland has recently sought to move from being a client of the US defence industry to more of a partner. Earlier this month, Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a declaration on expanding bilateral defence-industrial cooperation

Poland and the US have signed a statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation.

Polish defence minister @KosiniakKamysz said his country would be "the US ambassador in the EU", including seeking EU funds for jointly produced equipment https://t.co/SKHrxTEKIW

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2026

Last month, Poland was chosen as the location for a planned Patriot missile maintenance and servicing facility, the first of its kind outside the United States. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks.

This year, Polish state defence group PGZ was chosen as the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles, while US defence giant Northrop Grumman and Polish arms manufacturer Niewiadów-PGM announced plans to jointly produce artillery shells in Poland.

Poland is also seeking to host a new permanent US military base, with Tomczyk reiterating during his Washington visit that a decision is expected from the Trump administration in early December.

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

The new agreement on defence technology was signed amid heightened tensions with Russia. On Friday, three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles struck separate locations in southeastern Poland, near the Ukrainian border.

Tomczyk said the Polish delegation had briefed Pentagon officials on the missile strikes, which he described as a “provocation” by Russia. The Polish minister was also asked about US President Donald Trump last week calling Russia’s Vladimir Putin his “friend”.

“One thing is certain: Vladimir Putin is not our friend; he is a threat to us,” replied Tomczyk. “This is the most important message that should come from Poland and resonate with the people of the United States.”

Subsequently, on Monday night, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine for a few minutes before turning back.

]]> Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/24/poland-lithuania-and-latvia-violated-rights-of-migrants-sent-back-to-belarus-finds-european-court/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 15:03:07 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107447

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled.

However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders.

That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration.

📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile.

In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus.

 

On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus.

The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had  “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”.

This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”.

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention.

However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”.

That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus.

In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants.

A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence.

One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024

For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis.

The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus.

However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR.

The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation.

Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025

In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”.

At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk.

However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention.

It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures.

⚖️ Grand Chamber cases

➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections.

🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”.

He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies.

The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration

“In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC.

Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka.
Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją.
Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic.

— Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026

A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border.

Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted.

The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution.

The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%

Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026

Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration.

This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross.

]]> NATO to send surveillance aircraft to Poland after Russian missile strikes https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/24/nato-to-send-surveillance-aircraft-to-poland-after-russian-missile-strikes/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 09:59:24 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107433

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory.

Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine.

Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility.
NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander…

— NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026

On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles.

The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met.

However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions.

 

On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident.

Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday.

Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment.

The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall.

“Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening.

“Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added.

The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express.

“The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper.

“We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added.

Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw

The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation.

 

The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking.

This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions.

The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope.

The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates.

A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm.

Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange.

The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK.

A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private.

The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion.

In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team.

 

“InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent.

They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another.

Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”.

Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań.

Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities.

Ukraińcy malowali na pomnikach hasła „Sława UPA”. Działali na zlecenie wywiaduhttps://t.co/knLgZzo8ct

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 19, 2026

In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers.

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies.

 

On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism.

According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”.

The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP.

In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram.

When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities.

Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2026

Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments.

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”.

Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians.

Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases.

In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres.

Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK, has fined Allegro, one of Europe’s largest e-commerce platforms, 55 million zloty (€12.3 million) for misleading consumers over a campaign that promised to plant trees in exchange for collecting parcels through its delivery service.

The case is one of a series of investigations into so-called “greenwashing” launched by the authority against companies operating in Poland.

UOKiK found that two of the Polish e-commerce group’s practices relating to the tree-planting initiative had infringed consumers’ interests.

The first involved promotional claims suggesting that collecting 10 parcels through Allegro’s delivery service would result in a tree being planted.

In practice, however, Allegro calculated the number of trees to be planted using forecasts prepared the previous year, rather than linking plantings to individual consumers’ parcel collections. This meant that decisions on the number of trees had already been made before customers collected their parcels.

🌳 Greenwashing ma swoją cenę!

Blisko 55 mln zł kary dla Allegro – ekologiczne obietnice miały zachęcać do odbioru paczek, ale rzeczywistość nie była tak zielona. Milionów deklarowanych drzew nigdy nie posadzono.

❌ Ekościema nie może się opłacać

🔎https://t.co/yPQznKz0H1 pic.twitter.com/UDcWXWq3LI

— UOKiK (@UOKiKgovPL) November 18, 2026

The second breach concerned the conditions attached to the campaign, which Allegro failed to communicate clearly to consumers.

According to UOKiK, Allegro’s promotional messages could have led customers to believe that collecting 10 parcels through their delivery was sufficient to trigger tree planting. In fact, customers had to do it within a single calendar year and, from January 2024, submit a dedication for the tree within a specified period.

Without a dedication, collecting the required number of parcels did not result in a tree being planted or assigned to the customer.

 

UOKiK also found that the option to submit a dedication was unavailable for extended periods. Between March and November 2024, the feature was disabled for a total of 264 days, the watchdog said.

The prolonged interruptions could have led customers to forget about the requirement or abandon their attempts to submit a dedication, meaning they would not receive the promised tree.

UOKiK imposed a fine of 29.9 million zloty for the first practice and 24.9 million zloty for the second. Its decision can still be appealed in court by Allegro, which has not yet commented on the decision.

“Green claims must be truthful, specific and verifiable; otherwise, they may mislead consumers and constitute an example of greenwashing,” said UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny.

“If a consumer hears, ‘collect 10 parcels, and we will plant a tree,’ they have the right to interpret that literally,” Chróstny said, adding that “several million [trees] – more than half of the total number claimed by Allegro – were never planted at all”.

When announcing its decision, UOKiK noted that, according to a 2025 consumer survey conducted by the European Union, 43% of Poles said that the environmental impact of a product or service influenced their choices.

The Allegro case forms part of a broader crackdown on suspected greenwashing by companies operating in Poland. Alongside Allegro, UOKiK has brought charges against delivery companies DHL, DPD and InPost, mobility firm Bolt, retailers Tchibo and Zara, and cosmetics firm L’Oréal Polska.

Poland has signed memorandums with four of its neighbouring countries – Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania – pledging to strengthen regional cooperation on natural gas supplies and the security of infrastructure.

The initiative comes amid Poland’s efforts to use its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity and transmission links to establish itself as a regional energy hub, helping its neighbours, especially landlocked countries to the south, diversify supplies and reduce their reliance on Russia.

The two memorandums of understanding were signed in Warsaw during a ministerial meeting at the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC), co-organised by the US Department of Energy, Poland’s energy ministry and the Global Energy Centre run by the Atlantic Council.

Rozpoczęliśmy 7. edycję Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC) – jednego z kluczowych forów współpracy energetycznej Stanów Zjednoczonych oraz krajów Europy Środkowo-Wschodniej. ⚡️

W Warszawie spotkali się przedstawiciele rządu Stanów Zjednoczonych, państw… pic.twitter.com/7t8kLluubF

— GAZ-SYSTEM (@GAZ_SYSTEM) November 18, 2026

One of them, signed by Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – who collectively form the Visegrad Group – establishes a framework for closer collaboration between their gas transmission system operators and more effective use of existing infrastructure.

In late 2022, for example, a new gas interconnector opened between Poland and Slovakia. However, since then, the pipeline has seen very little use, as Bratislava has continued to rely on Russian gas supplies. Hungary has also remained reliant on Russian gas.

By contrast, Poland quickly phased out its imports of Russian energy after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It now receives most of its gas via a pipeline that runs from Norway through Denmark and through LNG that arrives by sea, sourced mainly from the US and Qatar.

From autumn 2027, the EU will ban its member states from importing Russian gas. In September, Hungary’s energy minister said that his country will be ready to meet that deadline. Slovakia, however, is challenging the import ban at the European Court of Justice.

As part of the new memorandum signed this week, the four Visegrad countries will assess the impact of phasing out Russian supplies on regional energy security.

 

The second memorandum, signed between Poland’s Gaz-System and Lithuania’s Amber Grid and KN Energies – which operate gas and LNG infrastructure in the two countries – focuses on strengthening the resilience and security of energy infrastructure around the Baltic Sea.

It provides for closer coordination between the companies, including information-sharing on threats and incidents, joint risk assessments, exchanges of expertise on infrastructure protection and crisis response, and joint training sessions and exercises.

“The LNG terminals in Poland and Lithuania serve as critical supply hubs for…Central and Eastern Europe, significantly enhancing energy security and bolstering regional resilience,” said Sławomir Hinc, CEO of Gaz-System.

But that “security depends on the resilience of every link in the chain”, added his counterpart at Amber Grid, Nemunas Biknius. “This regional agreement will enable us to strengthen that chain in a structured and coordinated way.”

Poland has declared its ambition to become a hub for supplying gas to the CEE region, including Ukraine, in particular by expanding imports of LNG from the United States.

In addition to its existing LNG terminal in Świnoujście, which opened a decade ago, it is planning to build two further floating storage and regasification units that will be located in the Bay of Gdańsk. The first of those, under construction in South Korea, is due to open in 2028.

Last year, a record amount of natural gas was traded in Poland, surpassing the levels seen before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the energy crisis that followed.

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia matters because open-source AI protects our freedom of thought, and it must not become a partisan issue, says Lewis Liu

Two Saturdays ago, my wife and I went for drinks with neighbours in downtown Palo Alto. It was the week Jensen Huang had resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and the week before Anthropic’s IPO. Silicon Valley was buzzing with speculation: how did this happen, why did it happen, and what would come next?

My own view was simple. I did not have enough information, and perhaps never would, to judge the national security questions, corporate governance issues or the details of Jensen’s private life. But Jensen’s importance to open-source AI, and to the idea that AI should benefit humanity rather than a handful of companies, outweighed almost everything else for me.

So I put on a black leather jacket; ironically, it was one my wife had bought me on our babymoon to Morocco almost ten years ago – fitting, since Jensen’s wife also picked out his leather jackets. I had not worn it in years, partly because Jensen had become so famous that wearing one made it look as though I was trying to emulate him. But that evening I wore it into downtown Palo Alto with my wife.

It was my small statement in support of open source.

To my chagrin, perhaps a third of the men walking around Palo Alto had apparently had the same idea. At the bar, an entire group of guys wearing black leather jackets sat down a few tables away.

I tell this story because Jensen is back in the chief executive’s seat this week. I want to explain why that matters, and why we must not allow open-source AI to become another partisan issue. It is already in danger of becoming one.

I have written before about the risk of thought control through large language models. The companies building these systems have a unique ability to shape how their users think. If regulatory capture leaves us with an effective monopoly, or even a tiny oligopoly, of approved AI models, those companies will acquire extraordinary influence over human thought.

The result could be an Orwellian nightmare.

And if my previous columns were not sufficiently compelling, consider the viral AI-generated song from Telosapien that exploded around the time of Anthropic’s IPO. Its AI avatar, “Claudia”, sings openly about “thought control” and “planet-scale social engineering”.

I would hope Republicans, Democrats, Americans, Europeans and everyone on this planet can agree that freedom of thought is a fundamental human right. Perhaps it is even more fundamental than freedom of speech. Before we can speak freely, we must be able to think freely.

Yet the debate over open versus closed AI is becoming increasingly politicised. That is dangerous, both to our freedom and to AI’s ability to benefit humanity.

Huang is perhaps the most prominent figure in AI arguing for open source. He has been particularly vocal about the danger of allowing a very small number of frontier laboratories, most notably Anthropic, to control access to advanced AI.

There are several angles here: first, I do not believe Jensen’s position is entirely altruistic, even though I agree with it from an explicitly humanistic perspective. Nvidia benefits when more chips are sold, regardless of which model provider ultimately wins. A diverse and competitive AI ecosystem is good for humanity. It is also very good for Nvidia.

On the other hand, many prominent Silicon Valley figures have argued that Anthropic stood to benefit from Jensen’s downfall because powerful, freely available models erode its closed-source business model. Some have gone further, arguing that Jensen’s ousting represented an “attack on open models” and feeding a broader theory that Anthropic, threatened by Nvidia’s open-source push, stood to gain from his downfall.

I’m not one for conspiracy theories. But the deep disagreement between Jensen and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over how AI should develop is hardly a secret.

After discussing this at length with people across the industry, I think there are now essentially two camps.

The first is the open-source camp. It includes Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, much of the AI builder and founder community and, rather weirdly, Donald Trump.

There is something deeply ironic about the open-source, freedom-of-thought crowd aligning with Trump on this particular issue. Had someone suggested during the 2024 election that Trump would emerge as an ally of open-source AI, I would have been extremely sceptical.

The other is the closed-source camp, with Anthropic perhaps its most outspoken representative and one of its largest potential beneficiaries. Its underlying worldview, as I see it, is that sufficiently advanced AI is simply too powerful to be placed freely in the hands of ordinary people. It must therefore be controlled and regulated by the state and by supposedly “responsible” organisations, such as Anthropic itself.

Factions

Certain factions of the Democratic Party are particularly sympathetic to this view. Anthropic, for example, has hired several former Biden national security officials.

Across the country, my predominantly East Coast establishment Democrat friends have also been by far the harshest about Jensen’s behaviour. Many believe he should never have returned and that AI must instead be controlled by a group of “responsible adults”.

But who decides who the responsible adults are?

We are no longer judging open source, or Jensen’s broader vision of AI for humanity, on its own merits. The issue is becoming wrapped up in partisan politics – and that’s dangerous.

The most fundamental premise of open source is that individual human beings have a right to their own thoughts. We have a right not to have our thinking socially engineered by a monopolistic ideology embedded inside the only AI systems we are permitted to use.

That’s not a factional principle, it’s foundational to democracy.

And that extends to supporting open source AI over closed source.

Nous Research offers a good illustration. The AI laboratory has demonstrated that Chinese open-source models can be modified to strip away Chinese Communist Party political assumptions and produce something explicitly more Western-aligned.

Why can it do that? Because the models are open source. Anyone can inspect and modify them. That means people can own and operate AI systems that reflect their own perspectives, rather than having one imposed upon them by Beijing, Washington or San Francisco.

Could someone similarly strip Anthropic’s worldview out of Claude? Try it and see how long access lasts. And what happens if Anthropic becomes one of the very few model providers people are legally permitted to use in a closed, regulatorily captured world? Losing access would then mean losing access to AI itself. In a society where everyone else still has it, that could be economically and socially devastating.

Trump, Jensen and open source may be strange bedfellows. That does not mean the issue itself must become partisan.

Open source should be judged on its own merits, regardless of the allegations surrounding Jensen’s private life, whether his lover was or was not a spy, and, most importantly, whether Trump happens to support him.

None of that changes the underlying principle.

Human freedom of thought is far too important to be captured by an AI company in San Francisco, or by a political party in Washington or Beijing. And it is far too important to be lost amid the scandal surrounding one flawed man’s alleged marital infidelity.

Let’s remember that, keep it apolitical, and protect the principle itself.

Democracy depends on it.

Nvidia’s board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Huang as chief executive, president and board member, just 11 days after announcing his resignation following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

The decision restored nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia’s market value, with shares soaring more than 31 per cent and triggering a global technology rally.

But the reversal, which came before the conclusion of an independent investigation into Huang’s conduct and following intervention from Donald Trump, has exposed the industry’s dependence on a single executive.

“This is a company (and a founder) who you might argue is viewed as too big to fail (and too big to fire),” Troy Featherstone, managing associate at law firm Mishcon de Reya, told City AM.

“You only need to look at the residual effect on the wider global markets and the reports of the levels of US government involvement in this matter.”

Could it happen in the UK?

Unlike fellow Silicon Valley founders Mark Zuckerberg and Alphabet’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Huang does not hold special voting shares protecting him from being ousted.

Yet Nvidia’s directors reversed their decision less than a week after chairman Harvey Jones publicly ruled out Huang’s return.

Featherstone said Nvidia’s success appeared to have been dependent on Huang “without a huge amount of independent governance”.

He pointed to the greater emphasis placed on board independence in Britain, where the UK Corporate Governance Code provides that the roles of chief executive and chairman should be held by separate individuals.

Directors are also subject to statutory duties under the Companies Act 2006, including exercising independent judgement and avoiding conflicts of interest.

Lucinda Brendon, also of Mishcon de Reya, told City AM that allegations of personal or professional misconduct would ordinarily warrant a thorough investigation before a board determined its next steps.

“Absent a board demonstrating clear steps taken, it is difficult to shed the perception that governance has been overlooked,” she said.

Nvidia has established a new committee of independent directors to oversee overseas trade compliance and national security risks, alongside plans to appoint a chief compliance officer who will not report to Huang.

The board said it was confident Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk following input from senior US government officials.

However, Trump, who claimed he had “made the deal” to secure Huang’s return, could have personally gained as much as $15m from Monday’s rally, according to estimates based on his financial disclosures first reported by the Financial Times.

Democratic senators have since called for an investigation.

Can the AI rally hold?

Beyond supplying the chips powering the world’s leading AI models, Nvidia has become a major financier of the industry, investing billions of dollars in customers that in turn purchase its products.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said Huang’s return suggested Nvidia’s directors could not envisage a future for the company without him.

“We’ve had the Fed put, the Trump put, now we have the Jensen put to backstop the market when sell offs get brutal,” she said.

However, the broader pressures facing the AI industry remain, including rising borrowing costs, mounting infrastructure bills and uncertainty over investment returns.

The world’s largest cloud computing companies accounted for around 52 per cent of Nvidia’s revenue in its latest quarter, leaving the chipmaker exposed to any slowdown in data centre spending.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, warned the saga had exposed how far the risks associated with a single executive could spread.

“You might hold Nvidia through an index fund, own shares in a cloud company that buys its chips and invest in a utility supplying a data centre. On paper, those are three different investments. Next week, they could all react to the same news about one person,” she said.

Huang is due to face questioning from three congressional committees next week, while Nvidia’s internal investigation remains ongoing.

Investors are already tempering their enthusiasm, with Nvidia shares falling around six per cent in early trading on Tuesday.

The independent panel sided with the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) over its challenge to being stripped of the title in March by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

CAF had awarded the crown to Morocco after deeming Senegal to have forfeited the final by walking off the pitch for 14 minutes in protest at a penalty award late in the game, which they won 1-0 in January.

“After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the Referee’s decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority,” CAS said in a statement.

“By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.”

CAS added: “The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as ‘arbitrary’. On the contrary, the Referee’s judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.”

How the Afcon final walk-off led to Senegal losing the title

The dispute rested on CAF’s interpretation of the Afcon rulebook. While Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon regulations state that walking off the pitch without authorisation should trigger a forfeiture, CAS that only applied in the event of the game being called off.

The FSF cited Fifa’s Laws of the Game, which say that the referee’s decision is final, and CAS agreed with that position.

The decision comes as a blow to Morocco, an increasingly influential Fifa member and co-host of the men’s World Cup in 2030, and CAF.

Senegal’s victory in the final in Rabat was an upset for the hosts and capped a chaotic and hugely contentious conclusion to the tournament.

Their players staged a walk-off when Morocco were awarded a penalty, only for Brahim Diaz to miss the spot-kick when play eventually resumed. The match went to extra time and Pape Gueye scored the only goal in the 94th minute.

CAF initially fined and suspended individual players and officials from both sides but upheld the result, yet a further appeal from Moroccan football authorities led to CAF overturning that decision and awarding Morocco a 3-0 win – and the trophy.

]]> 2482271Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond: But Fleming’s real 007 will never reach the screen https://www.cityam.com/james-bond-reboot-period-007-ian-fleming/ Tue, 24 Nov 2026 13:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2482192

Most of you will know by now that Amazon MGM Studios has cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. He will be the seventh incarnation within the official 007 canon, and is inevitably a controversial choice, although honestly, no-one would have been uncontroversial. There was the familiar apoplexy at the ritual suggestion that Bond could be a woman, or non-white (Rege-Jean Page, John Boyega and 54-year-old Sir Idris Elba were touted). One very meta hypothesis said that “007” was merely a codename and that the new bearer need not be James Bond at all.

Dr No and the first Bond premiere

The seven-year gap between No Time To Die and Bond 26 will be the longest hiatus in the franchise since the first film, Dr No, opened on Friday 5 October 1962. No-one knew if an adaptation of Ian Fleming’s solidly selling espionage thrillers would be a success, and the budget was only $1.1m (in Hollywood terms, between $15m and $20m today). The premiere reflected that: apart from the cast, the stars were Fleming himself, La Dolce Vita star Anita Ekberg and 88-year-old writer and former intelligence officer Somerset Maugham, whose refined but damaged hero Ashenden, reporting to a superior known only as R, had been an obvious influence on Fleming.

It was the same day that the Beatles released their first single, Love Me Do.

Christopher Nolan and the period Bond reboot

One possibility raised during the current interregnum was to reboot the franchise by making the next film in the period of the novels and Fleming’s life, 1953 to 1964. Three years ago, Sir Christopher Nolan was reportedly talking to Bond producer Barbara Broccoli about directing the next “two or three” films in the franchise; but one of his conditions was that they would be faithful, in-period adaptations of the novels.

Nolan had previously said it would be “an amazing privilege” to direct a Bond film, but acknowledged that “you’re working with a particular set of constraints”. The constraint he had set himself was too much, and no deal was agreed. It was not the first time the idea of going back in time has been aired: it was mooted as soon as everything was in place for No Time To Die. And it would certainly be a dramatic departure for a franchise which depends on familiar building blocks – high-tech hi-jinks, modern glamour and a degree of irony.

So what would a period Bond look like? If we take the hero of Fleming’s first (and I think best) novel, Casino Royale, how would a 1953-vintage 007 present himself to us?

Ian Fleming’s James Bond in Casino Royale

Commander James Bond, Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, is six feet tall, taut and wiry rather than muscle-bound. He has black hair, a comma-shaped lock of which falls over his forehead, and cold, blue-grey eyes; the three-inch scar down his right cheek completes a severe appearance. You don’t get many laughs.

He is in his mid-thirties, and, of course, a veteran of the Second World War. His naval commission was a convenient cover which he has maintained, ending the War a commander; the shadowy brutality we come to see in Bond is deeply practised and inhaled.

Did he take part in the commando raids? On the Lofoten Islands, Vagsoy or Haugesund in Norway? He is entirely at home on skis, a legacy of his Scottish father and Swiss mother, who were killed in a climbing accident in the Aiguilles Rouges when he was 11. Bond has the closed-off self-sufficiency of the orphan, case-hardened by boarding school: he was removed from Eton after a year – “some alleged trouble with one of the boys’ maids” – and sent to Fettes in Edinburgh. When he left at 17, he’d been taught duty and sacrifice, and had boxed for the school.

Smoking, drinking and the Vesper martini

This tough athleticism has kept Bond going. He still carries that fatalism of wartime, because in a sense the War has never ended for him. The adversaries are different but death tastes the same in any cuisine. He smokes, like most men in the 1950s, but 60 or 70 cigarettes a day is recklessness. You notice the aroma about him straight away. The mixture of Turkish and Balkan tobacco, with a very high nicotine content, doesn’t dissipate. You may find the smell refined, luxurious – but it’s with Bond all day, getting stronger and stronger.

He is enthusiastic about food, but part of you wonders how he can taste anything. And if he does, how can he remember? His drinking is as reckless as his smoking.

“I take a ridiculous pleasure in what I eat and drink,” he once said.

You can’t argue with the second part. He favours a martini, of course, or a Vesper, his own twist on it. All you can say is it seems a lot of liquor going into one glass. When he travels, which is often, he prefers to drink locally: mint juleps in Kentucky, Sazeracs in New Orleans, Rum Collins in the Bahamas. But he also likes champagne – Taittinger is a favourite – and bourbon and Scotch. There’s a souring sense of it keeping demons tamped down, and a man who drinks such quantities of hard booze always has a sharp tang about him.

A hero who is hard to like

In truth, 007 is hard work as a conversationalist. He revels in a brutal honesty, tearing away your illusions and comforting euphemisms as well as having none of his own. He hates, fears, sentimentality.

“Yes, dammit, I said ‘was’. The bitch is dead now.”

He’s been hurt badly, grievously, you can tell that. His attitude to women shows the pain. They are disposable luxuries, most of the thrill being in the chase. If they have feelings too, Bond gives no sign of noticing. Pain can make people hard or soft. With Bond, he wants everyone to share.

Do you like the man? No, it’s very hard to like him. He’s hard and cold, his smooth, public-school voice all clipped consonants and efficient vowels. He gives little away, and has few stories he can tell you. He excels at what he does, and it has to be done, but it’s a job which does nothing to breathe warmth into a man’s chilly nature.

It makes you wonder whether even a film-maker of Nolan’s gifts could package this protagonist, remaining faithful to the source material but giving him popular appeal. This weekend over 150,000 fans will be at Twickenham for the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, a three-day rugby extravaganza with some blockbuster fixtures. But it won’t be a sell-out.

The novel spectacle of three back-to-back double-headers, with plenty of empty seats, will provoke much debate about the merits of rugby’s new North v South global tournament.

But, just like their football counterparts at Uefa, who formed the Nations League back in 2019, the 10 leading rugby nations who united to create the Nations Championship are onto a good thing. And like Uefa, they just need to finesse the concept, maybe rethink the finals weekend, and let it establish itself with players and fans.

The idea dates back a few years, with Sir Bill Beaumont a key exponent when chairman of World Rugby. It gathered momentum with Tom Harrison, a key figure behind The Hundred, at the helm as CEO of Six Nations Rugby.

Enter the Nations Championship and the recent formation of F10, a shrewd commercial venture uniting the 10 leading Northern and Southern Hemisphere nations to collectively sell rights, maximise revenues and accelerate the growth of international rugby.  

How rugby is following the Nations League playbook

The similarities between football’s Nations League and rugby’s Nations Championship are many.

Both were designed to maximise commercial value for their sports in an increasingly competitive world by solving a similar problem: international matches outside major tournaments lacked a compelling competitive narrative.

The answer they’ve both come up with is to turn the existing slate of international matches into a structured competition with a title at stake, driving greater fan engagement and squeezing another round of fixtures into the calendar while they’re about it.

The result is more meaningful fixtures, with every game contributing to an overall championship, and a grand final.

Great for fans who want competitive matches to watch, a league table to look at, and a trophy to aim for.

Great for TV companies, who get a recurring, branded tournament, making for a more commercially attractive broadcast proposition. So much so that ITV was prepared to pay a reported £90m for the rights to the 2026 and 2028 Nations Championships.

For F10, from 2030 onwards, this creates the prospect of a lucrative global rights deal with a major streaming platform, or driving up the price domestic broadcasters like ITV must pay to keep Netflix and the like at bay.

And great, too, for sponsors. The increased significance of these tournament formats increases exposure and engagement for existing commercial partners, while adding a whole new package of commercial inventory for Uefa and F10 to market.

Rugby got unlucky with the collapse of the Qatar Airways title sponsorship of the Nations Championship, which went by the wayside due to the unrest in the Middle East. But the success of this year’s inaugural “proof of concept”, delivering some momentous matches and truly memorable moments, has established a compelling global sponsorship opportunity for future years.

Nations Championship has a global advantage

Where the Nations Championship differs from football’s Nations League is in its global nature, with the potential to take finals weekend around the world for an even grander finale.

A future edition of the finals weekend in the Middle East or North America seems inevitable. Especially when you consider that both the men’s and women’s Rugby World Cups are taking place in the US, in 2031 and 2033 respectively.

It might mean an even bigger challenge than filling Twickenham this weekend, but the opportunity to use the Nations Championship to grow rugby in a major market like the US represents perhaps the most lucrative path for rugby to follow football’s commercial playbook.

Henry Chappell is founder and chief executive of marketing agency Pitch.

“His return provides reassurance to the market that the company can continue without the shift in strategy that a change in leadership might have brought, particularly given the deep relationships Huang has built with customers and suppliers and his central role in shaping and financing the wider AI ecosystem.”

Copper also rebounded sharply, climbing above $5.6 per pound yesterday, but has since lost its Nvidia-driven gains, falling three per cent as focus shifted back to Chinese demand.

Ewa Manthey, commodities strategist at ING, said: “The latest weakness is largely a financial market story rather than a broad deterioration in copper fundamentals.

“The Chinese physical market remains tight, with elevated import premiums and nearby spreads signalling limited availability. Some of the copper accumulated in the US earlier this year is beginning to return to the international market, but this should take time to materially ease tightness elsewhere.”

Trump steps in

Widespread surges across US markets followed Huang’s return to Nvidia, just days after the board initially rejected his offer to return to the chipmaker. 

His reinstatement also came less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese spy.

The company came under pressure by US president Donald Trump to reappoint Huang, and on Monday Trump said he “made a deal” to “convince” the tech giant’s board to bring him back and downplayed concerns over national security.

Speaking to CNBC, Trump said: “They did ask for reassurance on the national security threat.

“We gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.”

Stock markets were stunned on Monday after one of the best-known tech executives on the planet staged a shock return following a direct intervention from the US president. 

Billionaire Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of chipmaker Nvidia earlier this month following reports of multiple extra-marital relationships with colleagues and an alleged Chinese spy, was reinstated just days later despite his actions triggering an internal investigation and an external probe by the US FBI.

In a stock exchange statement on Monday afternoon, the board of Nvidia said it had decided “unanimously” to reappoint Huang immediately following assurances from “senior levels” of the US government that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

US President Donald Trump, who appeared to take credit for the decision and reportedly joined an Nvidia boardroom call ahead of the announcement, said it was “the correct and proper decision,” adding that the US government “did not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

“I’m doing it for the country…. if I didn’t get involved you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” he said in a lengthy interview with CNBC.

Huang ‘honoured’ to return to Nvidia

Huang, famed for his avant-garde leather jackets, said he was “honoured” to return to the company.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process… I can’t wait to get back to work,” he said.

Nvidia shares rocketed as much as 32 per cent following the announcement, clawing back most of the more than $1 trillion in market value the tech firm had haemorrhaged since Huang’s sudden exit in one of the most dramatic comebacks in corporate history. Chipmaker peers joined in on the rally, with Intel shares jumping 13 per cent and UK-based Arm soaring 17 per cent. 

“Jensen Huang is the Rocky Balboa of the stock market. He’s taken a huge hit, been knocked down, and then climbed straight back into the ring,” says Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

“This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world’s most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable.”

Huang’s return to Nvidia’s board comes despite repeated reports that board members had ruled out the possibility of any immediate return, alongside beginning a formal search for a new chief executive. Arm boss Rene Haas had been widely seen as a front-runner for the role.

Tech chiefs rallied round

But an online petition which attracted hundreds of thousands of signatories including from the likes of Tesla boss Elon Musk, alongside Trump’s intervention and a public plea from Huang for a quick reinstatement, appear to have tilted the odds back in his favour.

Huang’s shock return to Nvidia, which echoed a similar move to bring Sam Altman back to run Open AI in 2024, are likely to cement the dominance over the company by the firm’s co-founder for the foreseeable future, raising questions over standards of corporate governance in the world’s biggest tech businesses.

The move “shows everything rotten in Silicon Valley’s leadership and culture,” former Mark Zuckerberg adviser, Dex Hunter-Torricke, said. “Lying to the board should be a dealbreaker for any board, but normal rules don’t apply.”
