]]> For decades, business leaders have been warned that the impending arrival of a new technology will completely reorder the corporate world. But for the best part of the last thirty years, it did not. 

The web, mobile phones, cloud computing and social media, for example, were all predicted as disruptors that would sweep the incumbents aside.

With AI, however, the warning deserves more consideration. The reason is less to do with the technology itself, but rather who is best placed to use it, and that is increasingly becoming startups, rather than established companies. 

The web didn’t break incumbents

The common story of the web is that of upstarts bringing down giants, and the rankings seem to agree.

The world’s most valuable company in 1995 was a Japanese telephone operator. In the same year, Microsoft barely made number twenty on the list and Nvidia was just a startup.  Today Microsoft, Nvidia, Apple, Amazon and Alphabet lead the rankings, and just six of the largest companies in 1995 remain in the top thirty. 

Though on closer examination, the incumbents were not the disasters the ranking implies. 

Companies such as Exxon, Coca-Cola and Toyota, more than tripled their combined revenue between 1994 and 2024, meanwhile Microsoft grew more than fiftyfold. The web gave them access to better logistics, cheaper computing and wider reach.  Oil companies could use better software without becoming software companies. Carmakers could run a more efficient supply chain. And a wealthier world could buy more cars, soft drinks and pharmaceuticals. The incumbents benefited from the technologies that were supposed to be disrupting them. 

It is therefore unsurprising that business leaders often meet warnings about AI with scepticism.

Where AI goes further than the web

The businesses that didn’t survive the dawn of the web, such as film rentals and newspaper classifieds, were not simply slow to adapt, they were substituted. The web typically made companies more productive rather than redundant.  

AI shifts this balance. While early digitisation took information and transactions online, real people were still responsible for interpreting information, exercising judgement and making decisions. AI can now take on a substantial share of that work. This raises the question of substitution again, but this time for jobs that sit inside offices, rather than on high streets. 

The startup advantage

The existing structure of established companies is built around human specialisation. Different departments and systems to coordinate different skillsets. While this structure made scale possible, it now makes it difficult to rethink how work can be done, which is why simply introducing AI into existing roles can often fall flat.

Startups have the benefit of starting from scratch, they can design their business around AI from the outset. A small team can now do the work of hundreds, and the ones who remain can serve customers, handle expectations and set the direction of the business. 

In the web era, startups predominantly sold tools to incumbents. Today, startups can enter the same markets as established players, but with fewer layers and at a fraction of the cost. The difference is design, not effort. Hospitals, nurseries and restaurants will always need their existing structures, but if your employees are knowledge workers, AI can be the foundation for a far more efficient and cost effective company. 

What decides the contest

Incumbents have spent decades building their customer trust, brand, proprietary data and deep expertise. While these are incredibly valuable assets, they are merely a headstart, not a guarantee. 

The contest will now likely become one of speed. Startups have to earn trust and knowledge, and incumbents must rebuild how their organisation works. 

The second task may be more difficult. Startups can earn trust through transparency and delivering good work. For incumbents, the challenge is to dismantle a structure that employs and rewards the people they  have to depend on to change it. 

Build the company that replaces yours

Rather than looking for ways for AI to improve their current organisations, business leaders should instead ask how they would build them today, with no existing structure. 

Incumbents should not throw away what they have already built, but they can decide which parts add actual value. However, that is also to say the organisational architecture that implements those advantages are blocking a new way of working.

So the question now becomes; if you were starting from scratch today, how would you build a company designed to put yourself out of business?

Then find a way to build it first.

US public charter operator JSX is planning to revive bankrupt New Pacific Airlines (NPA) under the JSX Air brand, with plans to launch a new operation using 42-seat Embraer ERJ145 regional jets.

In a filing submitted to the US Department of Transportation (DoT) on 20 November, NPA requested permission to resume operations under its existing air carrier certificate. It follows the acquisition by JSX of New Pacific Airlines, which was reportedly finalised in August.

JSX to operate as a Part 121 air carrier 

The proposed operation would see the company conduct public charter flights under Part 380 of the US Department of Transportation’s regulations, operating as a Part 121 air carrier. 

Services would initially concentrate on short-haul domestic routes of between approximately 200 and 300 nautical miles, with an emphasis on providing additional connections to smaller and mid-sized communities, the carrier said. 

NPA said the plan with JSX was to “provide passengers with a public charter jet experience at attainable fares, including personalised and attentive cabin service, business class legroom, complimentary snacks and drinks, and complimentary Starlink Wi-Fi”. 

It said the operation would be modelled on the proposition offered by its sister company, Delux Public Charter, which operates under the JSX brand.

Crucially, the new arrangement with NPA would allow JSX to operate an Embraer fleet with 42 seats. It is currently capped at 30 seats under Part 135 rules.

Bringing 42-seat Embraer ERJ145-LR into service

The carrier plans to introduce six Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft during its first year of operations. The aircraft are already operated by Delux and would be transferred to NPA through dry leases once the carrier is nearly complete with its Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certification review.

The DoT filing does not go into detail about initial routes for the new operation. 

However, NPA said it expects to expand its network over time, particularly to smaller and mid-sized cities. These are “communities that, in recent years, have seen declining levels of service from major scheduled airlines”, the filing stated. 

NPA is wholly owned by JetSuiteX, the parent company of JSX and Delux Public Charter. 

The company’s chief executive, Alex Wilcox, will also lead the revived airline.

How did NPA reach this point?

The move follows a turbulent period for NPA, formerly Northern Pacific Airways, which discontinued operations on 26 November 2025.

The carrier launched in 2022 with the express purpose of offering one-stop connections between North America and Asia using Boeing 757-200s with a stopover in Anchorage, Alaska.

Flights were planned from New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Orlando, and Las Vegas to Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya, Japan, as well as Seoul, South Korea.

In 2023, it was forced to change its name to New Pacific Airlines to avoid having to contest a trademark lawsuit.

The airline and several affiliates subsequently filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 26 January 2026, following mounting financial losses and unsuccessful attempts to restructure its debt outside court. 

The bankruptcy court approved a reorganisation plan on 18 August, under which JetSuiteX acquired the equity of New Pacific Airlines.

The new application sets out a first-year operating cost forecast of approximately $53.9m.

The company is seeking a waiver from the usual 45-day advance filing rule, arguing that it would allow NPA to offer “additional service to underserved communities and [bring] competition to a highly concentrated domestic airline industry” sooner than would otherwise be possible.

The post NASA takes ownership of X-59 as quiet supersonic flight moves closer to reality appeared first on AGN.

]]> NASA has officially taken ownership of the X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft from Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, marking another step in a programme that could eventually allow commercial passenger aircraft to fly faster than the speed of sound over land.

The transfer took place on 18 November and was announced by NASA on Monday, 23 November, following an aircraft acceptance review. Lockheed Martin will continue to provide technical support when required.

The aircraft has spent much of the past year demonstrating its flying qualities at different speeds and altitudes. NASA is now preparing for a more important part of the programme that of establishing whether the X-59 can consistently fly at supersonic speeds without producing the loud sonic booms that have restricted commercial operations over land for decades.

“To someone outside the flight test, this might seem like a subtle change,” said Cathy Bahm, NASA’s Low Boom Flight Demonstrator project manager.

“But for NASA, this is another big moment for the X-59, showing how far we have come, how much our hard work has paid off, and how much closer we are to providing the data to hopefully make commercial supersonic flight over land a reality,” Bahm said.

From 230mph to Mach 1.53 in a year

The X-59 made its maiden flight on 28 October 2025, taking off from Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works facility in Palmdale, California, and landing at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, which has since served as its operational base.

During that 67-minute flight, the aircraft reached 12,000ft and a speed of 230mph. The priority was to establish that its basic systems worked correctly and that the aircraft could be flown safely.

Following a scheduled maintenance period, the X-59 returned to the skies in March 2026. Engineers began gradually increasing its speed and altitude, studying how the aircraft behaved under different aerodynamic conditions.

On 5 June, NASA test pilot Jim ‘Clue’ Less took the X-59 beyond the speed of sound for the first time. The 81-minute flight reached Mach 1.1 at 43,400ft.

Less recalled that there was little to indicate from inside the cockpit that the aircraft had broken the sound barrier.

“You know you are supersonic when gauges say you are supersonic. I didn’t feel anything,” he said.

An even more significant milestone followed on 12 June, when the X-59 reached Mach 1.4 at 55,000ft. These are the conditions under which NASA intends to conduct its future flights over populated areas.

The distinction is important. The aircraft had now demonstrated that it could operate at the speed and altitude around which its low-boom technology was designed.

By August, engineers had completed 25 flights. NASA reported that measurements of aircraft stability, handling characteristics and structural loads were consistent with predictions made during computer simulations and wind tunnel testing.

No unexpected aerodynamic instability or excessive vibration had been encountered at that stage.

The pace of testing also increased. In September, the aircraft completed six flights in three days.

By the first anniversary of its maiden flight, the X-59 had completed 41 sorties, exceeded 56,000ft and reached a maximum speed of Mach 1.53. Its longest flight had lasted 102 minutes.

Why the X-59 looks so different

The unusual appearance of the X-59 is central to what NASA is trying to achieve.

When an aircraft travels faster than sound, pressure disturbances created as it moves through the air form shock waves. These can merge as they travel towards the ground, producing the familiar loud sonic boom.

The boom is not simply a noise generated at the moment an aircraft breaks the sound barrier. It continues along its supersonic flight path, potentially affecting communities hundreds of kilometres apart.

The X-59’s elongated nose, slender fuselage and carefully positioned wings are designed to prevent these shock waves from combining into a powerful boom.

Its engine is mounted above the fuselage, helping to reduce the shock waves directed towards the ground.

The design has also presented some unusual engineering challenges. The aircraft’s long nose leaves the pilot without a conventional forward-facing windscreen. Instead, cameras and a high-resolution cockpit display provide a view of the airspace ahead through what NASA calls the eXternal Vision System.

At its intended cruising speed and altitude, NASA expects the sound reaching the ground to resemble a car door being closed about six metres away.

Whether the aircraft can consistently achieve that level of noise under real atmospheric conditions is what the forthcoming tests will establish.

Has the X-59 demonstrated quiet supersonic flight yet?

Not conclusively.
Although the X-59 has flown beyond the speed of sound on numerous occasions, its early supersonic flights were primarily concerned with aircraft performance and safety.

A conventional NASA F-15 research aircraft accompanied those flights, allowing engineers to monitor the X-59 in the air. However, the F-15’s own sonic booms masked whatever sound the experimental aircraft produced.

NASA will now increasingly focus on acoustic validation, conducting dedicated flights within the supersonic test range around Edwards Air Force Base in California.

Researchers will measure the pressure waves generated by the aircraft and the sound they produce on reaching the ground.
Atmospheric conditions, including temperature and wind, can influence how those waves travel. Engineers therefore need measurements from a range of flight conditions before taking the aircraft over populated areas.

The public will have a say

Perhaps the most unusual part of NASA’s Quesst mission is that its eventual success will depend partly on people who have nothing to do with aviation.

Once acoustic testing is sufficiently advanced, NASA plans to fly the X-59 over selected US communities and ask residents about the noise they experience.

A sound that appears acceptable to engineers examining instrument readings may be perceived differently by people going about their daily lives.

NASA will collect those responses and provide the findings to US and international aviation regulators. The intention is to give authorities enough scientific evidence to consider noise-based restrictions rather than blanket prohibitions on supersonic flight over land.

The programme is currently scheduled to run through 2029.

What it means for supersonic passenger travel

Noise restrictions were among the factors that limited Concorde’s commercial operations, confining most of its supersonic services to routes over the ocean.

Since Concorde’s retirement in 2003, no commercial supersonic passenger aircraft has entered service.

Removing or substantially reducing the restrictions associated with sonic booms could open domestic and other overland routes to future supersonic airliners, potentially making them commercially attractive on a much wider network.

The X-59 itself is a single-seat research aircraft and will never carry paying passengers.

NASA intends to make the research, engineering tools and validated design methods developed through Quesst available to help manufacturers design quieter supersonic aircraft of their own.

]]> Who owns space? The short answer is no one; the long answer is considerably more nuanced.

As the United States, China and other countries pursue ambitious plans for the Moon, old space treaties are being tested by new technologies, commercial interests and growing competition.

Where does airspace end and space begin?

Article 1 of the 1944 Chicago Convention says every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory.

But a wrinkle is that the exact altitude at which airspace ends and outer space begins has never been formally agreed. The 100-kilometre Kármán line is widely used as a practical boundary, but it is not universally established in international law.

SpaceX’s Starlink satellites operate well above this, starting at 330 kilometres, while the 2023 Chinese spy balloon – shot down by the US – was flying at around 18km.

In practice, there is little disagreement about objects operating at aircraft altitudes or in orbit. The areas in between remain less clearly defined.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty: Why no country can own the Moon

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty remains the cornerstone of international space law.

Article II states, “Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means.”

In simple terms, no country can claim part of the Moon as its own territory. However, how some aspects of the treaty should be applied to future lunar settlements and resource extraction remains the subject of debate.

The treaty also establishes several other key principles. Outer space is free for exploration and use by all states, and countries cannot claim sovereignty over the Moon or other celestial bodies.

Nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction cannot be placed in orbit or stationed in outer space. Military bases and weapons testing are also prohibited on the Moon and other celestial bodies.

What can countries own in space?

While countries cannot own parts of the Moon, they do retain jurisdiction over their own spacecraft, satellites and other registered space equipment.

Think of it this way: a country cannot own a piece of the Moon, but it does own the lunar lander, rover or habitat it places there. This raises important questions for future lunar missions.

If one country builds a base on the Moon, can another country’s astronauts simply land beside it? Can they enter it? How close is too close?

In 2020, the United States and seven initial partner countries introduced the Artemis Accords to attempt to forge an agreement to establish common interpretations and practices of the Outer Space Treaty.

The accords have since attracted dozens of signatories, although major space powers including China remain outside the framework. Supporters argue the accords provide useful operational guidance, while critics say some provisions will ultimately require broader international agreement.

One of the most closely watched concepts within the accords is the idea of “safety zones” around lunar activities, intended to prevent harmful interference between operators.

Supporters say these zones would help prevent accidents and interference between missions. Critics worry they could eventually be used to create de facto control over valuable areas of the Moon.

Can anyone mine the Moon?

Commercial companies, including Blue Origin and SpaceX, have expressed ambitions to develop lunar infrastructure and exploit extra-terrestrial resources.

NASA’s Artemis programme and China’s International Lunar Research Station initiative, developed with different international partners, both envisage sustained infrastructure on the Moon.

India is often overlooked, but also has increasingly ambitious lunar exploration plans. Its government has announced a goal of landing an Indian astronaut on the Moon by 2040.

The law about extracting resources is also unclear. Article 11 of the Moon Agreement 1979 says the Moon and its natural resources are the common heritage of mankind. It adds that installing buildings does not establish ownership.

The agreement also notes that states would agree to establish an international regime to govern the exploitation of lunar resources when it becomes feasible. That time appears to be approaching, but it hasn’t been agreed.

The American 2015 Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act recognises American citizens’ rights to own resources they recover from space, while explicitly disclaiming sovereignty over celestial bodies.

NASA uses drone to test autonomous Moon and Mars landing technology NASA uses drone to test autonomous Moon and Mars landing technology

Limits of international law

There are several reasons why uncertainty remains.

One is that the Moon Agreement attracted relatively few signatories compared with the Outer Space Treaty and does not include many of the world’s leading spacefaring nations.

Another is that many of the core space treaties were written decades before permanent lunar operations or commercial space-resource extraction appeared technically or economically realistic.

As a result, different countries sometimes interpret the rules in different ways – particularly on issues that barely existed when the treaties were negotiated. For example, Saudi Arabia ratified the Moon Agreement in 2012, but later withdrew, with its withdrawal taking effect in January 2024.

Even countries that have not signed the Outer Space Treaty are generally expected to follow some of its basic principles. Exactly which rules apply remains a matter of debate.

Lessons from other international agreements

A useful comparison is Antarctica. The Antarctic Treaty allows countries to carry out scientific research without settling long-running disputes over territorial claims.

Space is different because the Outer Space Treaty prohibits countries from claiming territory in the first place. Even so, both agreements show how international cooperation can continue despite disagreements over ownership and governance.

What happens next?

The basic principle at the heart of space law remains clear: no country owns the Moon. The more difficult questions concern what happens around that principle.

Who can use lunar resources? How will different countries operate in the same locations? What happens if two missions want access to the same area?

Those questions are becoming more urgent as governments and private companies move closer to sustained operations beyond Earth.

For now, the basic rules exist, but many of the details have yet to be worked out. As human activity on the Moon grows, pressure will likely increase for clearer international agreements on mining, safety zones and the operation of future lunar bases.

]]> Russia could launch a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon as early as December, according to intelligence assessments cited by German media. Moscow has dismissed the reports about the spacecraft, known as Sputnik-S, and no launch has been confirmed.

But the warning raises a question for anyone who relies on satellites for communications, weather forecasts or navigation: what would happen if a nuclear weapon exploded in space?

The US got a glimpse of the answer in July 1962. Its Starfish Prime nuclear test lit up the night sky over the Pacific and knocked out about 300 streetlights in Hawaii. One of the satellites it damaged was still on the launchpad when the explosion took place.

Telstar 1 lifted off the following day and went on to relay television pictures across the Atlantic. Each time its orbit took it through the radiation belt left by the blast, its electronics received another dose. Within months, it began to lose contact with controllers on Earth.

Only a few dozen satellites were in orbit at the time of Starfish Prime. By January 2026, more than 13,000 were operating in low Earth orbit alone.

How a single nuclear explosion could cripple thousands of satellites

A study titled Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit, published on November 6, 2026, by researchers from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and Princeton University, examined the potential damage to today’s satellite infrastructure.

In one hypothetical scenario examined by the researchers, approximately 98% of the satellites modelled could be disabled within a week. The paper has yet to undergo peer review.

The danger would not end with the initial explosion. Electrons released in the aftermath of the detonation could become trapped in Earth’s magnetic field, creating an artificial radiation belt. Satellites repeatedly passing through this region would be exposed to radiation capable of damaging their electronics.

The researchers also examined the consequences of large numbers of spacecraft becoming uncontrollable. Disabled satellites would lose their ability to manoeuvre away from other objects, increasing the risk of collisions and the creation of space debris.

Even launching replacement satellites could prove difficult because radiation and debris might remain a hazard for years.

The authors warned that a single detonation could “devastate orbital infrastructure”, supporting efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.

What would happen on Earth?

Satellite failures on such a scale could disrupt internet connectivity, weather forecasting, maritime communications, disaster monitoring and military operations.

An electromagnetic pulse (EMP) generated by a high-altitude nuclear explosion could also damage electrical and electronic infrastructure on the ground.

Major General Armin Fleischmann of Germany’s Cyber and Information Domain Command told the journalists investigating Sputnik-S that the consequences for everyday life in Germany could include power outages and severe disruption to communications and navigation.

Modern banking, electricity distribution and telecommunications also depend on precise timing signals provided by satellites. Although GPS satellites operate in higher orbits than the spacecraft examined in the study, disruption to interconnected space and ground infrastructure could have consequences far beyond low Earth orbit.

Military forces could face the loss of communications, surveillance and intelligence capabilities. Civilian services that depend on satellite data could also be severely disrupted.

The effects would not respect national borders. Satellites belonging to neutral countries, commercial operators and potentially the country responsible for the explosion could all suffer damage.

When a nuclear explosion knocked out streetlights in Hawaii

The effects of Starfish Prime were visible across large parts of the Pacific. On the Hawaiian island of Oahu, about 900 miles from the explosion, fuses blew and around 300 streetlights went out. A microwave link carrying telephone calls between the islands was also damaged.

In orbit, the effects took longer to emerge. According to the US Army Space and Missile Defense Command, seven satellites were disabled following the test, representing approximately one-third of the satellites then in space.

Among them was Telstar 1. Engineers briefly restored contact with the pioneering communications satellite after radiation damaged its electronics. It fell silent for the last time in February 1963, more than seven months after the explosion.

Nuclear weapons in space are prohibited

The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibited nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, underwater and in outer space.

Four years later, the Outer Space Treaty explicitly prohibited countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit.

Russia vetoed a United Nations Security Council resolution in April 2024 that would have reaffirmed the prohibition on stationing nuclear weapons in space.

Moscow continues to deny that it intends to deploy such weapons.

Whether the reported Sputnik-S launch will take place remains unconfirmed. But the experience of Starfish Prime and the findings of the latest scientific study illustrate why the allegations have caused such concern. An attack on satellites intended to undermine an adversary’s military capabilities could leave civilian infrastructure across the world facing years of disruption.

“They honour our heritage while always looking forward,” said Antonio Fernandez Ojeda, Aeroméxico’s vice president of product and onboard services, of the airline’s design partner. The two companies have worked together for a decade. “This cabin programme is the boldest expression of that partnership: modern, calm and unmistakably Mexican, from the first row to the last.”

Aeroméxico’s announcement follows a similar move by Aer Lingus, which unveiled its first dedicated premium economy cabin, along with new business class suites and a refreshed economy cabin for its Airbus A330s.

What changes on Aeroméxico’s Boeing 787-8s?

Aeroméxico’s third-quarter results listed 25 Dreamliners in operation at the end of September, comprising 17 787-9s and eight 787-8s. Conesa said in Singapore that he expects the fleet to reach 30 by the end of the decade, including 22 of the larger 787-9s.

The smaller 787-8s will receive the Collins Aerospace Super Diamond business class seat currently used on the 787-9s. The variant will gain an upgraded business class seat, while the new suites and premium economy will debut on the 787-9.

]]> A Swedish Gripen fighter pilot was authorized to shoot down a suspected Russian cruise missile over Poland on 20 November – but didn’t fire because severe weather prevented him from positively identifying the target, according to a senior Polish military commander.

The pilot was attempting to intercept what was believed to be a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile during a major overnight attack on Ukraine.

Although NATO had granted conditional authorization to use weapons, the pilot could not confirm the object’s identity visually or through the aircraft’s electro-optical systems.

The details were disclosed by Lieutenant General Ireneusz Nowak, operational commander of the Polish Armed Forces, during a press conference.

The incident occurred as three airborne objects entered Polish territory during Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine. Polish authorities confirmed that nobody was injured and no damage to critical infrastructure had been reported.

Why the Gripen pilot did not fire

Two Swedish JAS 39 Gripen fighters were scrambled alongside Polish F-16s as NATO monitored several potential threats approaching Polish airspace.

The aircraft were operating under NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany, which issued conditional authorisation to engage identified threats.

The authorization allowed pilots to use weapons once the necessary conditions had been met, without seeking separate permission for each engagement.

According to Nowak, the Swedish pilot approached an object believed to be a Kh-101 cruise missile but could ot establish its identity because of exceptionally difficult weather conditions.

The pilot was unable to obtain the necessary confirmation using either visual observation or the Gripen’s electro-optical sensors and therefore did not fire.

Modern fighter aircraft use radar and other sensors to detect and track airborne objects. However, detecting a target does not necessarily establish its identity.

Radar can provide information about an object’s position, speed and direction, while optical and infrared sensors can help determine what it is. Poor visibility, cloud and precipitation can make that identification more difficult.

The Polish commander’s account did not indicate any technical malfunction involving the Gripen. The reported difficulty was identifying the target under the prevailing weather conditions.

Poland’s Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also addressed the broader considerations involved in engaging airborne threats.

“The decision is made by pilots and commanders after analysing the circumstances and the threat to the civilian population,” he said at the press conference on 20 November.

Swedish pilots tracked several targets

The Swedish Air Force confirmed that its Gripen fighters tracked several targets over Polish territory during an operation lasting several hours.

Deputy Air Force Chief Niclas Magnusson said Swedish pilots had operated in extremely difficult weather and visibility conditions.

“Last night, our pilots demonstrated Sweden’s ability to act, allied unity and the importance of our participation in the collective defence of Europe,” Magnusson said in a statement translated from Swedish.

“Together with our Polish allies, we scrambled quickly to defend our shared airspace.”

The operation required aerial refuelling in darkness and the servicing and preparation of Swedish fighters at a forward operating base in Poland.

Polish F-16s, a Saab airborne early-warning aircraft and a Dutch aerial refuelling aircraft also participated.

The Swedish Air Force did not identify the objects tracked by its pilots or report that any weapons had been fired.

Three objects entered Polish territory

The Polish Ministry of Defence said Russian long-range aircraft had launched Kinzhal and Kh-101 missiles, along with large numbers of jet-powered and conventional drones, during the attack on Ukraine.

Polish military authorities monitored 11 potentially threatening airborne objects, according to Nowak. Three entered Polish territory.

Debris or wreckage was located near Mołodycz, Rudnik nad Sanem and Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland.

Kosiniak-Kamysz confirmed that a Kh-101 cruise missile was found at Nowy Lipowiec. The other objects were provisionally assessed as another missile and a jet-powered drone.

He described the Russian attack as one of the largest since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“The most important information is that, as a result of the actions of the Russian Federation on Ukrainian territory, which affected Polish territory, no one was harmed in the Republic of Poland,” the minister said, according to an English translation of the ministry’s statement.

“We also have no reports of damage to critical infrastructure.”

Poland activated Patriot air defence systems around Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport and Swidnik, along with Poprad and Pilica plus ground-based systems.

Helicopters and three Territorial Defence Forces brigades were also involved in the response.

Poland seeks more NATO support

Kosiniak-Kamysz described the incursions as another Russian provocation and questioned their timing.

The incident coincided with COALITION 26.2, a multinational military exercise at Nowa Dęba involving members of the Coalition of the Willing supporting Ukraine.

“In my opinion, the date is not accidental,” he said.

The minister announced plans to request additional NATO forces and resources for Operation Eastern Sentry, launched in 2025 to strengthen the alliance’s eastern defences.

Sweden has been contributing Gripen fighters to NATO’s air defence operations since October. The aircraft are primarily based in Sweden during the two-month deployment but can also operate from a forward base in Poland.

The mission includes protecting southeastern Poland’s logistics hub, which supports military and civilian assistance to Ukraine.

 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 /* 2026-11-08: bar moved from bright brand blue (#0056b3) to the navy the
 homepage redesign uses (#12233D), so header, hero and institutions band
 share one anchor colour. To revert, put #0056b3 / 0.15 back. */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #12233D;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}

@media (min-width: 861px) {

 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}

 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {

 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;

 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {

 }

 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {

 }

#sie-auth-drawer,

 .lh-heroalt{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:10px;min-width:0}

 /* ── Make the search the priority, not an afterthought ────────────────
 Measured before this change at 1440x900: hero 1028px tall, search bar
 top at y=694. Tightened the vertical rhythm and moved the trust row

 .lh-hero.lh-hero{padding:clamp(28px,4vw,56px) 0 clamp(32px,4.5vw,64px)}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{gap:clamp(16px,2vw,26px)}
 /* ⚠️ THE CAUSE OF THE BIG EMPTY GAP, and it was mine. The stylesheet sets
 .lh-hero-text{flex:1 1 380px} and .lh-portals{flex:1 1 420px}. Those were
 written for the original ROW layout, where flex-basis is a WIDTH. Turning
 the container into a column silently turned both into fixed HEIGHTS: the
 text box stayed 380px tall although its content ended after 187px, and
 the search row stayed 420px tall although the cards are 195px. That is
 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}
 .lh-hero .lh-title{margin:0 0 12px}
 .lh-hero .lh-subtitle{margin:0;max-width:52ch}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{position:relative;z-index:1;margin:clamp(14px,1.8vw,22px) 0 0;gap:10px 24px}
 /* The bar itself carries the emphasis: taller, larger type, and a navy

 paper it was the loudest thing in the hero. Scoped to .lh-herosearch so
 the same widget elsewhere keeps the brand button. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-bar{min-height:64px;padding:4px 6px 4px 14px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-input{font-size:17px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn{background:#12233D;border-color:#12233D;color:#fff;font-weight:600}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn:hover{background:#1E3354;border-color:#1E3354}
 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}
 /* The flow view (AI matching on) groups results into one .sie-flow__branch

 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.
 The first keeps padding-left:0 so its numeral lines up with the margin
 the hero headline uses. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-num{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(27px,2.9vw,40px);font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;line-height:1.05;color:#12233D;background:none;-webkit-text-fill-color:currentColor}
 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}
 @media(max-width:700px){
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr))}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:nth-child(2){border-right:0}
 }

 .lh-inst{background:#12233D;color:#fff}

 .lh-inst-badge{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-h{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(26px,3.1vw,40px);line-height:1.16;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;color:#fff;max-width:20ch}
 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}

 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}
 /* The accent word: italic navy reads editorial; bright orange read promo. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-gradient-text{color:#12233D;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D;font-style:italic;font-weight:600}
 /* One label above the headline is enough. The H1 eyebrow ("STUDY IN
 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}
 /* Phones: the hero had no side gutter, so the eyebrow sat flush against
 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text,.lh-hero .lh-subtitle{text-align:left}
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 }
 /* ── Section headers: same voice as the institutions band ─────────────
 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-header h2{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px) !important;letter-spacing:-.4px;line-height:1.15;color:#12233D !important}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-how{background:#FAF8F4}
 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 /* How it works: the three steps were top-aligned, so the middle card
 (longer text) hung lower than its neighbours. Stretch evens them. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-steps{align-items:stretch}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step{background:#fff;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}

 .lh-wrap .lh-step-arrow{color:#B7B1A5}

 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─

 the loudest part of the page. Same content, one navy, warm neutrals.
 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__source-pill{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;box-shadow:none !important;border-radius:4px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch{--branch-color:#12233D !important;--branch-bg:#F4F2ED !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-accent{display:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-icon{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card{background:#FAF8F4;border:1px solid #EDEAE3;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card:hover{border-color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel
 (blue / yellow / blue) via !important rules at .lh-uni-card:nth-child()
 specificity, so this needs one more class to win. Plain paper, so the
 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.

 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;

 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

{"data":[{"slug":"technical-product-manager-munich-85258","company_name":"Sanovio","title":"Technical Product Manager","description":"

About SANOVIO<\/h2>

SANOVIO is the collaborative AI platform for healthcare procurement. Every euro a hospital loses in purchasing is missing in patient care. We help hospitals get good products at fair prices, with far less manual work.<\/p>

We build the software. And we move the goods. SANOVIO aOS, our agentic operating system for procurement, handles master data management, portfolio management and digital procurement processing. SANOVIO Fulfillment covers global direct sourcing, quality control, warehousing and logistics.<\/p>

Founded in 2024 in Munich by Noel Nosswitz, Alexander H\u00fcttner and Yong Wang, we work with hospitals in Germany and Switzerland, purchasing groups and international suppliers. We are customer-funded: our customers are our only investors.<\/p>

The role<\/h2>

As Technical Product Manager, you turn real procurement problems into working software. You sit between our hospital and supplier users, our engineering team and the founders. You decide what we build next, shape how it works, and often build the first version yourself.<\/p>

You work on SANOVIO aOS and the internal tools behind our fulfillment operations: AI agents that clean item master data, workflows that move an order from request to ward, and integrations with hospital and supplier systems.<\/p>

A large part of the role is talking to customers. You join calls and on-site visits with hospital purchasing teams, purchasing groups and suppliers, show them what we build, take their feedback and turn it into product decisions. You are a trusted contact for our customers on everything technical.<\/p>

Location: Munich (on-site, with flexibility).<\/p>

What you will do<\/h2>

  • Own the product roadmap for selected areas of SANOVIO aOS, from problem discovery to release.<\/p><\/li>

  • Be in close, regular contact with customers: hospital buyers, purchasing groups and suppliers, plus our own operations team, to understand how procurement works in practice.<\/p><\/li>

  • Lead the implementation of SANOVIO aOS at customers: from setup and data onboarding to go-live.<\/p><\/li>

  • Own product education: run trainings and onboarding for customers and our internal teams, and create guides and demos.<\/p><\/li>

  • Write clear product specifications and translate them into tasks engineering can ship.<\/p><\/li>

  • Understand and map user flows end to end, and find where users lose time or get stuck.<\/p><\/li>

  • Iterate fast: ship a first version, learn from real users and improve it within days, not months.<\/p><\/li>

  • Design and prototype AI agents and LLM-based features, for example matching products across supplier catalogues or checking certificates.<\/p><\/li>

  • Automate internal workflows across procurement, quality, warehousing and finance, and connect the systems behind them.<\/p><\/li>

  • Define how we measure success for each feature and follow up after launch.<\/p><\/li>

  • Make sure what we build is secure, reliable and handles confidential hospital and supplier data with care.<\/p><\/li><\/ul>

    Technical Skills<\/h2>

    • Strong software engineering fundamentals, including practical experience with Python, APIs, databases and modern development tools.<\/p><\/li>

    • Hands-on experience developing AI-powered applications using large language models, AI agents and related technologies.<\/p><\/li>

    • Experience implementing workflow automation and integrating different software systems and data sources.<\/p><\/li>

    • Understanding of software architecture, data processing, deployment and the development of reliable, maintainable applications.<\/p><\/li>

    • Familiarity with information security, access management and the responsible handling of confidential data.<\/p><\/li>

    • Experience with modern AI-assisted development tools and an interest in continuously expanding your technical expertise.<\/p><\/li><\/ul>

      What else you bring<\/h2>

      • A degree in computer science, engineering, business informatics or a related field, or equivalent practical experience.<\/p><\/li>

      • Graduates are welcome, as are candidates with 1 to 2 years of work experience.<\/p><\/li>

      • A background in consulting (for example strategy, tech or operations consulting) and a strong pull towards AI: you build with LLMs and agents yourself, not only in slides.<\/p><\/li>

      • Experience in product development: you have taken a product or internal tool from first idea to something people use every day.<\/p><\/li>

      • Experience in customer-facing work: you enjoy presenting to customers, running workshops and explaining a technical decision to a hospital buyer as clearly as a business problem to an engineer.<\/p><\/li>

      • You take ownership, work in a structured way and are comfortable when things are not yet defined.<\/p><\/li>

      • You are AI-native: you use AI tools every day and follow what is new in the field.<\/p><\/li>

      • You care about healthcare and want your work to have a visible effect on patient care.<\/p><\/li>

      • Fluent English and German at C1 level or higher, as many of our customers work in German.<\/p><\/li><\/ul>

        What we offer<\/h2>

        • A real problem with a direct effect on patient care.<\/p><\/li>

        • AI that acts: you ship agents that do real work in procurement, not demos.<\/p><\/li>

        • Software and logistics in one company, so you see your product used from order to ward.<\/p><\/li>

        • A lot of responsibility from day one, real ownership of your area and short paths to the founders.<\/p><\/li>

        • An office in the heart of Munich.<\/p><\/li><\/ul>

          How to apply<\/h2>

          Apply here with your CV and your LinkedIn profile. A link to your GitHub, portfolio or personal website is optional.<\/p>

          About the Role<\/strong><\/p>

          As a Founding Engineer<\/strong> at SANOVIO, you will play a key role in building the AI-powered procurement infrastructure that tackles one of the biggest and most complex cost problems in European healthcare.<\/p>

          This is a fast-paced, hands-on role for engineers with high agency<\/strong>, strong technical depth, and a founder mindset. We\u2019re looking for a full-stack generalist<\/strong> with a strong frontend affinity<\/strong>. You excel at designing user flows<\/strong> and implementing them in React and TypeScript<\/strong>, while owning outcomes end-to-end across backend, data, AI-enabled workflows, and cloud deployment<\/strong>. You thrive amid uncertainty and incomplete requirements<\/strong>, move quickly, and still care deeply about architecture, clean code, and long-term quality<\/strong>.<\/p>

          If you are a passionate builder who thrives at the intersection of full-stack development and AI, this is your opportunity to work closely with the founders, shape the product, and help us scale toward \u20ac10M ARR in 2026<\/strong>.

          Tasks<\/strong><\/p>

          • Owning end-to-end product workflows<\/strong>, from frontend UX to backend systems, data pipelines, and edge cases<\/p><\/li>

          • Building world-class frontend experiences <\/strong>in React and TypeScript alongside scalable, reliable backend systems<\/strong><\/p><\/li>

          • Designing and owning AI-enabled systems<\/strong>, including embeddings, retrieval, and agents that create real operational leverage<\/p><\/li>

          • Developing and operating data pipelines<\/strong> for large-scale unstructured data<\/p><\/li>

          • Making pragmatic technical decisions on architecture, tools, and frameworks<\/strong> to balance speed and quality<\/p><\/li>

          • Deploying, running, and maintaining software in cloud environments<\/strong> with a \u201cyou ship it, you run it\u201d mindset<\/p><\/li>

          • Writing clean, maintainable, and well-tested code with scalable, reusable components and APIs<\/strong><\/p><\/li>

          • Collaborating across the stack<\/strong> and raising the engineering bar through reviews, mentoring, and technical leadership
            <\/p><\/li><\/ul>

            General Profile<\/strong>

            We are looking for stellar engineers with a strong background in full-stack software engineering and AI<\/strong>, and the potential to grow and lead teams in the future. 3\u20135 years of experience is a plus<\/strong>, but we hire for skill, ownership, and output.<\/p>

            • Generalist engineer with a frontend affinity, capable of building across backend, data, and AI<\/p><\/li>

            • End-to-end product ownership, driving ideas from concept to customer-ready production<\/p><\/li>

            • Proactive execution in ambiguous environments, turning unclear requirements into shipped software<\/p><\/li>

            • High-speed delivery paired with a focus on clean code and scalable architecture<\/p><\/li>

            • Close iteration with users and clients, including collaboration across different cultures<\/p><\/li>

            • Strong problem-solving ability and fast adoption of new technologies<\/p><\/li>

            • Motivation to build excellent software in a fast-paced startup environment<\/p><\/li>

            • Willingness to work in-person in Munich with a higher intensity than a traditional 9\u20135 role<\/p><\/li><\/ul>

              Technical skillset<\/strong><\/p>

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What You Will Do<\/strong><\/p>

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              \u203a Own the delivery of the project design from initial brief through to detailed design, ensuring design deliverables meet the agreed scope, quality, budget and programme requirements.<\/p>

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              \u203a Establish and maintain the project design brief with customers, Product, Engineering, Operations and Delivery, capturing requirements, scope boundaries, acceptance criteria and responsibilities.<\/p>

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              \u203a Develop and manage the design delivery programme, aligning design packages, reviews, approvals and information release with key project milestones.<\/p>
